subtopic: PROPOSED PAYMENT OF DEPOSITORS TO THE AMOUNT OF $5,450,000

speechtext:
Hon. J. A, ROBB (Acting Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide for the payment out of the consolidated revenue fund of the sum of five million four hundred and fifty thousand dollars for the purpose of paying to the several persons who were creditors of The Home Bank of Canada for money on deposit or in current account such proportionate part of the amounts for which they are determined to be creditors in the liquidation proceedings as the said sum will provide, and to authorize the Governor in Council to raise by way of loan such sum as may be required for the purpose of making the payment aforesaid.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the resolution upon, which will be founded a bill, provides for partial payment-about thirty-five per cent-to the depositors of the Home Bank of Canada. The Canadian banking system provides for the double liability of all shareholders of a bank, provides for the redemption at par of the bank notes authorized and issued by a Canadian bank, but does not provide guarantee of deposits. I emphasize this fact so that it may be clearly understood that under our system of banking, and indeed under most of the backing systems of the world, governments do not guarantee deposits. Canadian chartered banks are required to submit to the government sworn statements of their position. We have now government inspection of banks. Every care is exercised to protect the public. But the law makes it clear that deposits are not now, and never have been, guaranteed.
The resolution, and the bill to be introduced, is to implement what many people regard as a unanimous order from the members of this House, under date of the 17th of July, 1924. It is presented to parliament in this form, so that this House, which in July, 1924, unanimously approved the report of the Banking and Commerce committee, may now have an opportunity of sharing the responsibility of the measure proposed to discharge what the Banking and Commerce committee regard as a moral claim.
The Home Bank of Canada closed its doors on the 17th day of August, 1923. A petition was presented in the month of January, 1924,

to the government, praying for a grant for the relief of the depositors. An order in council was passed on the 27th February, 1924, appointing Hon. A. J. McKeown, Chief Justice of the Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick, a commissioner under the Enquiries Act to make an investigation into the affairs of the bank at and prior to the date of the failure. The report of the commissioner was duly presented to the House of Commons and referred to the Banking and Commerce committee. The report of the Banking and Commerce committee thereon was presented to the House of Commons on the 1st day of July, 1924, the concluding paragraph being as follows:
Your committee consider that the facts brought out in the interim report submitted by Mr. Justice McKeown and the evidence therein referred to establish that the depositors of the Home Bank have a moral claim in equity for compensation by the country on account of any loss they may suffer by reason of the failure of the Home Bank.
On the 17th cf July the report of the Banking and Commerce committee in this behalf was unanimously concurred in by the House. Subsequently, on the 18 h July, the Prime Minister, in the House of Commons, after quoting the concluding paragraph of the report hereinbefore set out, stated that the government would give careful consideration to the report which had been accepted unanimously by the House and at the next session of parliament would make an announcement as to the extent to which, in their opinion, parliament should be asked to recognize the moral claim which in the report it is stated the depositors of the bank have.
The amount of the claims of depositors, owing to adjustments -which are being made from time to time by the liquidator, have not yet been settled in the liquidation proceedings. The net amount that will be due to persons in the position of depositors when the list of creditors is finally se'tled by the court will be approximately $15,500,000. The government proposes that, as outlined in the resolution, a payment of $5,450,000-equal to about 35 cents on the dollar,-be placed in the hands of the liquidator for distribution among the depositors. This will enable the liquidator to make a distribution of approximately thirty-five per cent of their claims to- the deposi: ors. The depositors have already received a payment of twenty-five per cent through the liquidator. While it is not yet possible to determine what the remaining asse's of the failed bank will yield, the liquidator anticipates that there will be a further payment of at least ten per cent from the

Home Bank
asets. That means that from the assets and this payment, if authorized by parliament, the depositors of the failed bank will receive approximately seventy per cent of their claims. [DOT]

The Home Bank
failure is one of the greatest "black marks" which banking in Canada has ever experienced. In looking at its early history, my judgment is that this bank should never have received a charter. The charter was granted to a concern that was at the time practically bankrupt. Having received the charter, the management seem to have proceeded to wreck the institution and was not unsuccessful. The principles of good banking were ignored; deception and fraud were practised; so that in the end shareholders, depositors and others suffered severe loss. There was a period when this government could have saved heavy loss to those interested parties, the depositors and shareholders, without costing the country a dollar. But they did not do so; they allowed the bank to go to the wall. Now the country is called upon to provide some five and a half millions to reimburse the depositors who unfortunately made a bad investment by placing their savings in that bank. This is a dangerous policy, forming a precedent and opening the door for further claims, past or future, of similar character. The government is not legally liable; it is not the duty of the government to pay the losses of people who have made mistaken investments. No government should be expected to guarantee any investments, and governments and parliaments have in the past repeatedly set their faces against any such guarantees. It is fundamentally unfair to take the moneys of all the people, in this case by way of taxation, for the benefit of some few people who happen to be Home Bank! depositors. Speaking as a member representing a constituency in Nova Scotia, the people of which province have not a single interest at! stakey T consider it is palpably unfair to call upon them for money for the benefit of people in Ontario and further west. They should not be asked to reimburse those who have unfortunately lost their money. Nova Scotia has experienced more than one bank failure; the Maritime provinces have experienced bank failures; but did the depositors or shareholders appeal with hat in hand for charity to ibe reimbursed for those losses? Never. Therefore, it is palpably unfair to ask that part of the country to contribute towards reimbursing those who

have unfortunately lost money in the Home Bank. I sympathize very sincerely with those who have made losses, with anybody who has made losses. Generally speaking, we find that the introduction of amendments leads to confusion rather than otherwise, and) they are the means of turning our thoughts away from the main issue. I would oppose the amendment for the further reason that it is not a matter that has been before this parliament. While many members of this parliament may be familiar with the circumstances surrounding the failure of the Farmens' Bank, it must be remembered that this is a new parliament and while we have given some Consideration to the question of the Home Bank, we are naturally not in a position at the present moment to consider the question of the Farmers' Bank. I would oppose the amendment also, because this difference lies upon the surface, that the reason that is advanced for the introduction of the present bill-that this is the outcome of certain conditions that prevailed during the war-does not apply as regards the Farmers' Bank. That reason on the surface is sufficient to make a distinction between the two cases. Those who hold that the depositors of the Farmers' Bank have a just claim against the government should present their claim to parliament when we shall deal with it on its merits. For my part, I accept this bill in the same spirit as the hon. member for Dufferin (Mr. Woods) and the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell). I wish some consideration could be given to the suggestion made by the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), who introduced a new thought into the question. He intimated that there was a possibility that speculators had already been at work. We certainly do not want to do anything to encourage the speculator. If there are those who have been taking advantage of the necessities of the depositors and advancing money to them in the hope that later on they will be reimbursed, we should take steps 
to see that those gentlemen get nothing more than the actual amount that they have advanced with such interest as may be deemed fair It would be quite possible for us at this time to make a provision that would cover that matter. I can readily see the difficulty that arises when a suggestion is made that there should be discrimination in the payment of depositors. It has been suggested that all sums under $1,000 should be paid in full. It can easily be understood that that would not conduce to equality. It might be that a very large corporation or association or some wealthy man happened to have a small deposit in the Home Bank and other persons, some of whom I know, had all their savings, perhaps some $3,000 or $4,000 or more in that bank, and to pay the one in full and the other in part would be failing absolutely to apply the principle of equity. If any means can be arrived at, any instructions given to the liquidators that would ensure that those who are most in need of relief are to be attended to first, certainly we would like to see that done. But at a glance anyone can see the difficulties that will confront them in arriving at conclusions in the matter. speechtext:
I am willing to accept this
legislation which has been brought down, but I would have preferred if the amount had been placed in the estimates. There is one 253

feature that has not been touched on in the discussion that has taken place to-day, and that is this. The depositors in the Home Bank are in a little different position from those of any other bank that has failed, so far as I know. I believe it was pointed out by the report of Chief Justice McKeown that if Sir Thomas White had taken action in 1916 the depositors would not have lost one cent. I may be wrong about that, but I believe I am right. And there is a difference between the failure or the poor judgment of a minister and his deliberate and1 calculated act. I will not say that Sir Thomas White was wrong in taking the course he did in the interest of Canada as a whole. I think possibly I might have taken the same course, but as a result of his not taking action at that time, the depositors were placed in a position to lose a very heavy sum of money, and as Canada as a whole gained thereby, it is right and perfectly proper, I think, that Canada as a whole should pay.
If possible I would like to see the suggestion that has been made-that the money be distributed according to the need of the depositors-acted upon, but I am afraid that if any attempt were made to do that, it would simply open the door to dissatisfaction. The question would arise, what about the need- the need at the time the bank closed, or the need now? Some depositors may be much poorer at the present time than they were when the bank closed. The more one thinks about it, the more clearly one sees that it would open the door to dissatisfaction. While the suggestion is a good one, I am afraid that it could not be carried out without causing a lot of dissatisfaction. I think it would be better to distribute the money in proportion to the amount on deposit at the time the bank closed its doors. I am afraid I must vote against the amendment because it confuses two issues. Each of these should be brought before the House separately and judged on its merits. For these reasons I must vote against the amendment, and for the bill.

I am compelled to say something on this bill owing to the remarks made by my hon. friend from Saskatoon (Mr. Evans) as to the criminality of this and other governments; I suppose he meant, in that connection, the minister. In the first instance, I would like to see if there was any criminality. We will be frank and go right back, because I know the hon. gentleman is talking about 1916, and what he thinks should have been done then and was not done, and
Home Bank

then in a burst of wild imagination he said that anyone responsible for that should be treated just like some other criminals who are now behind the bars, or words to that effect. I would just like to tell the hon. gentlemen in the first place, that I think the hot weather has affected him-
Not at all.

-because generally he is much more sensible than that. If Sir Thomas White made any mistake in 1916, I want to tell my hon. friend, there are an awful lot of people in his part of the country who made the same mistake. After all, what did Sir Thomas White do? In the year 1916 he accepted the advice and the judgment of Hon. Mr. Crerar, who, if anybody ought to know anything about it, ought to have known about this matter. That is what happened; nothing else happened. You can talk as much as you like about the war. Of course, the war made it just that much more difficult. I thought somebody might be foolish enough to bring up this question, and therefore I took one or two notes as to the proceedings, and I am going right into what really took place.
In the first instance, I point out that in 1916 the complaint was made to the hon. Minister of Finance, then Sir Thomas White. From whom does that complaint come? That complaint comes from the western directors. And who are the western directors? They are Messrs. Crerar, Persse and Kennedy. In connection with their complaint they go into the whole thing. They give a wealth of detail; they go into different accounts; they show where losses are likely, and complain of management and the like. Papers are received, and the question of going into the whole thing is considered. These people who make the complaints, these people who ought to know; get busy to find out what can be done. Why, Hon. Mr. Crerar comes down here and re-arranges the management. He brings out Mr. Haney and replaces Colonel Mason. More than that, the same hon. gentleman makes valuations of collateral; he goes out to British Columbia and makes a valuation of collateral, and reports to Sir Thomas White that in connection with those large lumber accounts, instead of there being a loss on them, there is a comfortable balance.
I am going to refer to the evidence. I am going to ask the House if any reasonable man in the possession of his senses- and here I do not accuse the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans), because I put it down to the weather although he says it is not-would not do just as Sir Thomas White

did. I will tell the hon. gentleman again now, so that it will not be overlooked, that on the express request of Hon. Mr. Crerar, Sir Thomas White took no action. Did Sir Thomas White do anything unreasonable in complying with Mr. Crerar's request? Was there anything about Mr. Crerar that the hon. member for Saskatoon is going to suggest ought to have put Sir Thomas White on his guard? Was not Hon. Mr. Crerar a man whose word hon. gentlemen, and particularly hon. gentlemen to my left, would say ought to be taken? Let us take for granted-I think we have a right to do that -that Sir Thomas White was right in looking upon Mr. Crerar as a man of his word, a man of integrity, a man of ability. Does anyone want to challenge that?
Let us see now whether he had any speteial knowledge in connection with the Home Bank. I submit-and I think the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woods-worth) will agree with me that there was nothing about Mr. Crerar to put Sir Thomas White especially on his guard against him; and if the hon. member does not agree with me, other hon. members will. They will agree that Sir Thomas White was right. If there was anyone who knew about the Home Bank it was Mr. Crerar. Why, he put the Home Bank on the map in western territory. A director of years' standing, having to do with the sale of the stock and the issue of the prospectus, why, surely to goodness, Mr. Chairman, if there was any one man in the world that Sir Thomas White had a right to think knew about this matter and whose word could be taken, it was Hon. Mr. Crerar, more particularly in view of his standing. Is Sir Thomas White to be blamed throughout the west because he believed in Hon. Thomas Crerar? That is the case put by the member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans).
Now, as I say, Mr. Crerar, with his company, the United Grain Growers Limited, had to do with the Home Bank for many years. I am going to ask hon. gentlemen to look at page 582 of the evidence taken before Hon. Mr. Justice McKeown. They will there find that the Grain Growers' Grain Company Limited acted as selling agents for the Home Bank in disposing of the stock, and that they got a commission of five per cent. And I may tell the hon. gentleman that they proved themselves to be good people of business. Looking at the daily press, I notice that out of 1,800 shareholders, there are 1,100 located in western Canada as a result of that selling agency. So they did pretty well. They issued a prospectus, and there is no doubt again about this; the hon. gentlemen will find

Home Bank
it at page 583 of the same evidence. I am going to read a short extract from the Grain Growers' prospectus:
Take this opportunity of getting in on the ground floor, not of a visionary bank, but of one strongly established and paying good dividends. Let us have a Home Bank which would be the people's bank. Read this prospectus, and learn about it and think about it.
The Grain Growers' Grain Company believed in the bank. They were not trying to get rid of something they did not believe in; why, they owned a thousand shares of the bank stock at that time And Mr. Crerar believed1 in it too; he owned sixty-six shares. So far as I am concerned, I have no doubt about the honesty of Mr. Crerar in the representations he made to Sir Thomas White, any more than I have the slightest doubt at all as to the honesty and correctness of Sir Thomas White in believing that Mr. Crerar was telling the truth and knew something of what he was talking about. That is the whole issue; there is no other issue.
The western directors' complaint is dated January 22, 1916. Then Mr. Crerar, as I said before, takes an active part in reorganization. He goes himself and inspects and values the collateral, and after all his activities down here, on March 20, 1916, he writes Sir Thomas White as follows:
Sir Thomas White,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa, Canada.
Home Bank of Canada
Dear Sir,-You will have learned from Mr. Lash of our visit to Ottawa to-day to discuss bank matters with you, and our faillure to see you through your absence from the city. You will also have learned of the change made at the recent meeting of the Board held in Toronto a few days ago, whereby the active management of affairs is placed in entirely new hands through Mr. Haney taking the vice-Presidency, and assuming direct executive control, with Mr. Machaffie, the Manager in Winnipeg, whom, for the time being at least, he is bringing to Toronto to assist him. By this arrangement I feel quite certain that the knowledge and information concerning the position of affairs desired by the Western Members of the Board, and also the changes they desired when they directed their request to you, and which they saw no hope of securing through the then existing management, can now be satisfactorily obtained without calling in outside assistance. In my opinion, the situation has materially improved within the past month, and, at this juncture with the changes in management recently made, it is better to have the enquiry proceed from within rather than from without.
Owing to the possibiflity of my being unable to attend a suggested conference with you next week, I am giving this letter to Mr. Lash so that he may place it before you. I may add that Mr. Kennedy, with whom I have discussed the views herein expressed, is in agreement with them. Mr. Persse, the other Western Director, is in the South, and so we have been unable to consult him. I feel however, that were he here he would be in agreement with us.
I am,
Yours truly,
T. A. Crebab,
353i
There is the letter of protest. There were also interviews, requests, demands, that this bank should not be driven to the wall and destroyed, but should be given an opportunity of carrying on without the publicity thait an outside investigation would engender. My hon. friend now wants us to believe that it was a criminal act because Sir Thomas White listened to Hon. Mr. Crerar-for that is what he did, nothing else. This attitude was persisted in by the Hon. Mr. Crerar, and right down until after the smash, according to his evidence before the investigator, that was still his attitude. He was not taking anything back; it was still his belief; and I will give hon. gentlemen some other pages of the evidence where they can find' it. Perhaps then they will say something more about Mr. Crerar. For example, referring to the May meet-ing-the May meeting subsequent to the writing of the letter of March-in his evidence at page 431 Mr. Crerar says:
At this meeting I remember, at the end of May, there was a decidedly optimistic feeling. The western directors felt satisfied with the energetic manner in which Mr. Haney was taking hold of things.
Again, according to the evidence, his opinion remained unchanged. Why, Mr. Crerar himself sold part of his stock in 1918, and he sold the balance in March, 1923. These sales were made after he resigned from the board. Hon. gentlemen will remember that he resigned on entering, the Union government. In answering a question put to him in connection with these sales, at page 487. he savs:
I had no more inside information than any of the other directors had. I had been off the board for over six months-
This is when he is asked why he sold his stock.
-and I want to say now, Mr. Reid, and I want to make it perfectly clear to you and to the court, that at that time I thought the bank was getting into a good position, and I did not sell my shares if your question implies that, because I had a doubt as to what might happen to the bank.
Again on page 488:
Q. What reason had you to think the Home Bank of Canada was all right at that time?
That is, the time when the stock was sold, as late as 1923. His answer is:
Because I had confidence in the management of the bank at that time, and I thought its position was improved.
There is Mr. Crerar's testimony. Honestly- and it is just as well to be honest with ourselves sometimes, if we cannot be with anybody else-honestly, who ought to know more about the affairs of the Home Bank in 1916, the man who gets the formal reports and the formal complaint, cr the man who makes the
Home Bank

formal complaint, the man who was looking after the sales of the stock?
Why does not the hon. gentleman refer to the general manager of the Home Bank instead of to Mr. Crerar all the time? The general manager knew the whole inside story.

My hon. friend
is making an interruption. He can talk as much as he likes a little later on. But I do not mind answering questions. I am not saying that Sir Thomas White stopped this investigation because he was told anything by the manager. If I said so it would be untrue. The reason he stayed his hand was because of what he -was told by Hon. Mr. Crerar. There was no crime in Mr. Crerar's telling him that. What I am saying to-day is justified, and necessarily so, by the remarks of the hon. member for Saskatoon.

Who' knew better than
Hon. Mr. Crerar? The general manager knew better.
The general manager was under a cloud; Mr. Crerar had made his charges against him-that it was necessary he should be got rid of. 'He was in process of elimination, and he was eliminated.

Did Sir Thomas White not
know at the time?

Know what?
All Sir Thomas White knew was that Hon. Mr. Crerar had made complaints to him; that Mr. Crerar had been a director for six years and was in a position to know what was going on-or should .be if he had been carrying out his duity, as I assume he was-at any rate, Sir Thomas White had a right to assume it. The general manager was the man under suspicion, and the very worst thing to do would be to go to him. Mr. Crerar says, he must be got rid of. Mr. Crerar reports he is got rid of; there is a new management; all is well; keep your hand off our institution. And because thait is done, hon. gentlemen suggest that Sir Thomas White should be behind the bars. Well, there is the action taken by Sir Thomas White on the strength of what he got from Hon. Mr. Crerar, and I submit that Sir Thomas White was perfectly justified in taking that action, just as Hon. Mr. Crerar was perfectly justified in doing what he did. Hon. Mr. Crerar was honest, I think, in every single thing he did in that connection. But because a minister of the crown believes in a man of the standing of Hon. Mr. Crerar, a man who knows the business, a man who makes a complaint and then says, "Stay your

hand, it is all right,"-anyone who makes a suggestion that that was improper on the part of the minister is not doing himself justice. What was there about Hon. Mr. Crerar that would put Sir Thomas White on his guard? What was there about his morals or his standing to make Sir Thomas White think he was not a man fit to consult with, that he was not a man whose word could be taken?
Nothing.

Nothing; the
hon. gentleman is perfectly right. I think Hon. Mr. Crerar went into that thing with the best of motives; I think he sold the stock with the best of motives; I think 5 p.m. he wanted to build up the concern properly, and that his complaint was absolutely right. Moreover, I think he was right in going around and making his valuations and the like, though it turned out he was wrong-
Does the hon. member seriously contend' that the responsibility of the Minister of Finance ended with the assurance from one of the directors that the affairs of the bank were in better shape?

The situation
was this:	The position of the bank is drawn
to his attention by the three western directors. He takes the question up with them and they arrange for a change of management. They are satisfied that they can pull the bank through, and he happens to believe it-he happened to believe that they could pull it through and that they should be given a chance. What other responsibility is there except to take the reports as they are put in from time to time? Was he to believe that all these reports were false, as subsequently turned out? His whole liability was confined in the first instance to what was referred to in that complaint. The complaint being settled the way it was; and the reports being what they were, what else was there? There was at that time no inspection of banks, there was no right to go in and pull them about in all directions as there is now. There was then no highly paid official giving all his time to going about among the banks and getting the facts. What else could Sir Thomas White do? He could either put the bank out of business, or he could say, "Mr. Crerar is a pretty good chap; I am going to give him a chance to pull this institution out of the hole"-and he did it. I have given you Mr. Crerar's evidence and have quoted his letter. It is of no use to base an argument upon doubt or surmise; here are the facts. Now, the next question is, did Sir Thomas White act rightly-

Home Bank

The hon.
member has based his argument on the suggestion that action was taken wholly on the responsibility of Hon. Mr. Crerar. Does he think that Sir Thomas White, then Minister of Finance, gave no consideration to the effect the failure of the bank would have on the affairs of the country ait that critical time, and that that did not influence his judgment in the matter?

There is ample reason without it. With it, of course, the situation1 is complicated. But I ana not going to give my own opinion, nor shall I merely use newspaper reports, and that sort of thing, where many loose things are said; I will refer to the evidence itself.

I have not
the evidence before me. Is that not in the evidence?

Haney report with regard to New Orleans, in view of the opinion expressed by Mr. Crerar, and his fellow directors from the west, what would they have said in 1916 if I had closed up the Home Bank?
Yes, and' we might stop here and ask what would the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans) have said at that time if Hon. Mr. Crerar had been turned down and a western bank put out of business? Why, the eohoes from the yell that would have gone up from those eleven hundred shareholders would be still ringing.
Down here we did not catch the sotto-voce remarks of the leader of the opposition.

I was just emphasizing
the well spoken words of the hon. member for West York. I commend them earnestly to the hon. member for Brome.
I was listening carefully.

Sir Thomas
White goes on:
Well, I know what they would have said. They would have advocated appointing a committee for the minister, that is what they would have done. What would they have said about the value of the timber limit? What would they have said about New Orleans? What would they have said about the goodwill of that bank built up over twenty years? The goodwill of a bank is worth millions sometimes. In the case of the Merchants Bank it was said to be worth seven millions. The goodwill, the establishment, the money spent, the effort made, the advertising, the connection, all lost if you close a bank.
Now, I think that very fairly answers the question put to me by the hon. member as to what Sir Thomas White acted upon. As to the outside inquiry of 1916, he acted upon representations made by Hon. Mr. Crerar, and in the judgment of any fair-minded man in this country he had to act upon those representations, unless he was of opinion that Hon. Mr. Crerar was such a man that no reliance could be placed upon his statements. I should think hon. gentlemen would be very slow in making such a suggestion as that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I would not
for a moment assume that my hon. friend from Glengarry and Stormont who has moved an amendment wishes to defeat the resolution before the committee and thereby deprive the depositors of the Home Bank of any relief. I point out to him, however, that without in any way helping the depositors of the Farmers' Bank such can be only the effect of his amendment.
In the first place, as my hon. friend knows, the matter of compensating the depositors of the Farmers' Bank has been before this House and has been before the upper chamber, and

with respect to that ibank the Senate has already expressed its view and' opinion. My hon. friend, I think, may logically assume that if a bill based on this resolution goes to the Senate with his amendment to compensate the Farmers' Bank depositors as well as the Home Bank depositors the only effect will be to have the bill defeated.
Mr. KENNEDY (Glengarry and Stormont!: Would the government welcome that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, the government would not welcome it. The government expects this legislation will pass the Senate and wants it to pass. The government has had no purpose in bringing this measure into the House other than to carry out what it believes to be its honourable duty in view of the finding made by the commission that investigated this matter, and in view of the unanimous report of a committee of the House. I want to make that perfectly clear because that is the ground on which the government has proceeded.
Perhaps I may be permitted to recall the circumstances under which this matter came before the government. As hon. members will recall, the depositors of the Home Bank appointed a national committee to wait upon the government and present certain grounds on which they claimed the right to have their losses made good in so far as the government could see its way to recognize their claim. They presented two grounds on which they based their claim. One was that the Minister of Finance of the day had taken a certain course for patriotic reasons, had pursued a course which was detrimental to the depositors because he believed it was in the interests of the country as a whole. The other ground was that the minister of the day had not performed his duty, that he had been neglectful, that he had not complied with the requirements of the law; and it was said by the depositors on either of these grounds we are entitled to have our losses made good. The government might have reached a decision of its own volition. To have done so would have 'been to judge a political opponent. The government would have been called upon to pronounce judgment on Sir Thomas White, minister of a former government, as to whether has action was in the nature of a patriotic act, or whether it was a neglect of public duty. The administration did not feel it would wish, in a matter of such importance, to have itself put in that position for a minute. We therefore took the one course that would remove the discussion of the Home Bank matter entirely from the realm of partisan politics by appointing a royal commission, asking the parties to

Home Bank
appear before the commission to present their statement, allowing the commission to make its findings; and when the commission had made its report, the government transferred the report to the committee of this House that has to do with Banking and Commerce. That committee had opportunity to consider the report very carefully, and it brought in a recommendation that upon the evidence taken before the commissioner it was of the opinion there was a moral claim in equity. This House passed that report unanimously, and it is on that action that the government to-day is basing its position, not upon any other ground or upon any other reason. We have not wished to go into the question of whether Sir Thomas White's action was one of patriotism or neglect of duty; we have not wished to open up any matter that could be regarded in any way as a subject of political controversy. We are prepared to accept the report of the commission, and the committee, and in good faith we have brought down this measure after carefully discussing all aspects of it with the liquidator who knows more about the affairs of the bank and its depositors than any other living person.

Did the commissioner
find there -was any moral claim in equity or legal claim against the country?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He found there was a moral claim.

Where?
Mr. MACKENZIE KING; That was the nature of the finding.

I do not know where he
found it. I would like my right hon. friend to refer to it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think if my hon. friend will study the report of the committee-
It is not there.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
-he will find
it in the report that the committee brought in to the House; the particular finding which he has just read was based on the report of the commissioner.
There was no such finding in the commissioner's report at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Well, the exact words were not there, but I am giving the inference which the committee drew from the finding of the commissioner.

Did the commissioner find that the
former Minister of Finance had not done his duty?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not want at the moment to go into what the commissioner found in regard to that matter. All I wish to make clear is that the finding of the commission was placed before the committee of this House, and the committee of this House had a right to inquire into every phase of that finding.

The minister referred to two grounds on which the legislation was based, first that of the neglect of the former Minister of Finance, and secondly, patriotic reasons. Did the commissioner find in regard to those two reasons?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I said that
these were the grounds that were urged before the government, and that the government refused to entertain either of them. The government said, "We will not pronounce judgment upon a political opponent. We are not here to say-and it is not our duty in a matter of this kind to say-whether Sir Thomas White performed his duty or did not perform it, but what we do feel is that the importance of the case, having regard to the arguments presented to us, is such that we should appoint a royal commission to investigate this matter and prepare a report for the consideration of parliament." When that report was prepared it was submitted by the government to the standing committee of this House dealing with Banking and Commerce, and when that committee had the report before it and had gone into the merits of the report, they brought to this House their finding that there was a moral claim in equity on the part of the depositors of the Home Bank against the government. We have endeavoured to implement what we believe to be the obligation of the government, in view of the report presented to us. As I was saying, the liquidator probably knows the position of the depositors better than anyone else. All the suggestions that have been raised this afternoon were raised by the Minister of Finance and myself with the liquidator when discussing this bill with him, and were very carefully considered 'by the cabinet as a whole. I think many of us felt, as the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) has expressed himself this afternoon, that if the measure could be made
Home Bank

one of caring particularly for distressed cases, those who have suffered obviously, the less fortunate members of the community, as contrasted with those persons who may be well to do, we would for many reasons prefer to proceed in that way; but the finding of the committee was that there was a moral claim on the part of the depositors against the government. The finding dlid not say a moral claim by the man who had a small account, or by the man who had a large account or by the miner, or by the municipality. It merely said a moral claim on behalf of the depositors; the government was obliged to act with respect to a moral claim; is it possible to permit a claim of one depositor and deny it in the case of the other? Having considered that matter very carefully, and more particularly having had a knowledge of the clas3 of depositors on the whole, it seemed to us we were perhaps, in the bill to be introduced, coming nearer to doing what my hon. friend has suggested is desirable than could be done in any other way. May I illustrate? My hon. friend has spoken about the case of the miners in Fernie. He said they should obviously be a first consideration of the government in a matter of this kind. If one were drawing a contrast between an individual who should be paid, and a group who should not be as favourably treated, one would be inclined to say that a corporation was well able to take care of itself. It so happens that the municipality of Fernie is one of the corporations most involved dn loss through its deposits in the Home Bank, and as one studies the situation, one finds that in Fernie the ratepayers of the Fernie corporation are almost completely the miners themselves and the one mining corporation that employs them. To deny the corporation of Fernie any consideration in this 'matter would be to injure the very class my hon, friend says we should be careful to consider in a matter of this kind. When it comes to a case of considering the corporation of Femie, and not considering the corporation of Toronto; for example, which had a deposit in the Home Bank, would this House have looked favourably upon any action on the part of the government whicfh would have approved compensating losses in the 'case of one corporation and denying similar rights to another. I can assure hon. members that in considering this claim the government has gone carefully over the whole situation and weighed every aspect of it, with the idea of meeting the obligation of the moral claim in what seams to be the most equitable manner.

May I say a word as to the other point which has been mentioned, namely, the propriety of the government bringing in this measure in the form of a bill? Some criticism has been made to the effect that we should have placed the amount in the estimates. First of all, may I say in regard to that, so far as this .parliament is concerned, I have yet to learn of any case where moneys, other than for the public service, or based upon some ball which has passed this House, or upon some resolution of the House or one of its committees, have been appropriated in the form of estimates. Estimates are generally for the public service. However, apart from that, may I draw attention of the House to this circumstance? If we had brought dn this measure by way of an estimate, or had asked parliament for an 'appropriation through an estimate, the very first criticism of hon. gentlemen apposite would have been that we were denying to another branch of this parliament which has a right to pass on. matters of public 'policy the right to consider a great question that affects the interests of the taxpayers of Canada and the people of Canada as a whole, and that we could not be supported in so doing. We would next have been asked why we had departed from the precedent set by hon. gentlemen apposite when they undertook to compensate the Farmers' Bank depositors. They did not proceed by way of estimate, but they took parliament as a whole into their confidence and brought in a bill which passed this House and went to the other 'chamber. True that bill did not pass there. We hope this bill will meet a different fate. But the circumstance that parliament, in dealing with matters of this kind, had previously proceeded by way of a bill rather than by estimate was a strong reason why this government should not in a matter of practice depart from a precedent already set in this House.
But there is another aspeot of this situation and another reason I want to give this House very frankly which made it impossible for this government to have proceeded by way of an estimate, ilf it wished to do so, in preference to bringing in a bill, and that wais the nature of a report made to us, to members of the government, by a committee of the depositors that waited upon myself and some other ministers in presenting Claims on their behalf to the government. They intimated to us that what was equivalent to a threat had been made that if the government did not proceed by way of an estimate, it was taking a course which would sknply mean that its purpose would not foe carried out. I asked

Home Bank
what the committee meant by a repnesemta-tion of that kind. They stated that they had been told1 by an hon. member of the Senate, one who was leading his party in the Senate, that if the government were to brinig in this measure in the form of a bill, that bill would be defeated in t'he Senate.
Does the right hon. gentleman refer to Sir James Lougheed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Sir James
Lougheed was away ill at the time. Senator Robertson is the gentleman to whom I refer, a member of the Senate who was leading the Conservative party in the Senate during Sir James Lougheed's absence from the other House. Senator Robertson intimated to the National Committee of Depositors that if the government proceeded by way of a bill, that bill would be defeated in the Senate-an extraordinary procedure for an hon. member of another House to undertake to speak for that other House as to what action it would take on a bill presented to parliament. What right had he to say what action the Senate was going to take on a public matter? What right has any hon. member of the Senate to deny to the Senate the fullest consideration and discussion of a matter of this kind? Having regard to a threat such as that, the government had no alternative, even had it wished to take any other course, than to proceed in the manner in which it is proceeding at the present time.
I think the Prime Minister ought to go a little further. He ought to tell us where he got that information. If he is making a charge against Senator Robertson, he ought to be a little more explicit.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I told my hon. friend I got it from the committee who made representations to me that they had received it from Senator Robertson.
From every member of the committee?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
From the members of the committee who were present. I was not satisfied with that. I said to the members of the committee: I Want a little more substantial evidence. I was just like my hon. friend in that regard. They therefore gave me Senator Robertson's letter which I shall read to the House. The letter is as follows:
The Senate Canada
Ottawa, 27th February, 1925.
Dear Mr. Lee,-
May I acknowledge, with thanks, receipt of your letter of the 11th February enclosing a statement
outlining the opinion of the Home Bank Depositors' National Relief Committee, in support of government action of relief to the depositors.
I think I have in previous letters outlined to you quite clearly my present views which were and are that the Home Bank was conceived in iniquity, born in dishonesty and never was conducted as it should have been from the beginning. When it was inevitable that the bank should close its doors and the matter was brought to the attention of the federal government, no effort was made to safeguard the depositors' interest, let alone the bank's credit, by the government, notwithstanding the fact that substantial relief had been given by the government in other instances which would have been ample to have saved the situation in this case, and this unfavourable consideration by the government resulted in the crash occurring.
These are facts in addition to those brought out during the investigation which you conducted before a commission appointed for the purpose.
As previously stated to you I have always been of the opinion that a much stronger case could have been made out, had it not appeared to be that every effort was being made to avoid embarrassing the present government in any way and the interest of the Home Bank depositors suffered in consequence thereof. I therefore have no hesitation in saying to you frankly and openly that if the government is in earnest in its professed desire to provide a measure of relief for Home Bank depositors it should include in the estimates of the present session of parliament whatever amount it desires to contribute for that purpose. Estimates as you know, are wholly within the jurisdiction of the House of Commons and are not subject to revision or modification by the Senate. You also are aware that notice has already been given to the effect that if relief is granted to the Home Bank depositors, notice of the demand for similar relief for depositors in other banks which have previously failed in Canada would be made. This contention, with much supporting evidence from quarters in Canada where other banks existed and failed will undoubtedly be brought to bear in the Senate if the government propose its measure of relief through a special bill, and it naturally is uncertain what the result of the legislation might be.
However, I reiterate that if the government is sincere in its desire and intention to aid Home Bank depositors it should include whatever amount it desires to contribute in the estimates where it ought to be and not by way of a special bill.
Yours sincerely,
G. D. Robertson.
Mr. W. T. J. Lee,
Chairman Home Bank Depositors' Relief Association, 244 Bay street, Toronto.
That letter does not support the Prime Minister.
Not at all.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen opposite applaud.	I wish again to repeat what I have said. I think it is a most extraordinary thing that the leader of the Conservative party in the Senate should make a declaration to the Home Bank depositors that if any measure goes from this
Home Bank

House with respect to the Home Bank, that measure is going to be killed in the Senate.
Some bon. MEMBERS: He does not say that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I hope my hon. friends will read this letter over just as carefully as the country will read it. When a letter of that kind was presented to this administration, no matter what the wish of this administration might have been, no government that was worthy of the name would take a defiance of that kind from the Conservative party.
Pretty free interpretation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have often
said that I think the powers of the Senate in some, if not many particulars, should be modified. I think the furthest I have ever gone with respect to measures emanating from this House is that if bills had passed this House on three successive occasions, they should become law whether the Senate rejected them or not. But, I have never taken the position that the Senate is not a second chamber in this parliament and has not as such powers co-equal with those of this House with respect to most measures of public importance. With regard to a. measure of this kind which affects all classes in this country, it is of the utmost importance that it should be presented in the form of a bill. Indeed, if this government had denied the Senate the right of discussing this measure, what stronger weapon against any Senate reform would it have been possible to have placed in the hands of those who would like to see the Senate in its powers remain as it is? The people as a whole have certain rights which should be conserved, not only in this House but in the Senate as well. It is only when the Senate by its action repeated over and over again obviously defeats what is the will of the people's representatives in parliament, that the Senate's action in any essential particular should be controlled. '
I wish to repeat the government has brought in this measure in the form that it has so that there would be no room for criticism on the part of hon. members opposite, either as to the method of bringing about this relief, or as to the fairness of the method by which the government has proceeded, or as to the justice of the whole situation before the country. We have taken a course that cannot be criticized in any particular, in the belief that in the Senate there are a sufficient number of hon. gentlemen who will be prepared to view this matter in the light in

which we have viewed it, and who will see that the action which this House takes will also be taken by the upper chamber.

It has always been the practice in each of the two branches of parliament to be scrupulously careful as to attacks on hon. members of the other body. This is essentially the part of fairness. It is essentially the part of dignity.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I would point out to my right hon. friend that I have not attacked any utterance of Senator Robertson's in the other chamber. I have in my hand a letter which was written to a committee apart from anything which was said in the Senate. I have made no reference to any utterance or debate in the other chamber.

I had not reached the point where the interruption was pertinent. Notwithstanding the fact that the utterance may not have been made in the other body, no matter where it may have been made, this has been the invariable practice of both branches of parliament. It has been so for the very obvious reason that the other party to the controversy is not here to take part in his defence.
I would just call the hon. gentteman's attention to this fact: I was attacked, I think it was a year ago, in a most vicious way by name in the upper chamber.

I would be very sorry to see the rules violated, especially as against the Minister of Railways, and still more sorry to see a vicious precedent followed by the Prime Minister. But when the incentive to the attack is a letter read this afternoon by the Prime Minister, I wonder what hon. gentleman would feel himself competent to describe such conduct as that, a letter which was in advance proclaimed to be a declaration that if the government brought forward relief in the form of a bill it would be defeated in the Senate of Canada; and the appeal was made to this House to know what is to be thought of a senator who dares to say what is going to happen to. a measure in the upper house, to appropriate to himself the right to declare what one branch of parliament will do. The letter was read, and it was found to contain not one word, not one syllable, of any such assertion of authority on the part of 'Senator Robertson. Senator Robertson evidently felt, and I know he has always felt, that a money vote of this kind should take its place with money votes of all kinds, and that if it did so take its place

Home Bank
it was an evidence of sincerity behind that vote on the government's part. Whether he is right in that contention or not may be debatable, but that is his view. But to make a personal attack upon him because he expressed it, would seem to me to be something a private member would not be proud of, and that a Prime Minister should lament. That the view is shared by very many in this House, there is no question. That it was expressed by many hon. gentlemen opposite themselves in the debate on the Farmers' Bank there is equally no question-this view for which Senator Robertson is taken to task and denounced to-day in his absence.
There is something to be said for a bill in relation to a measure of this kind, but it cannot be said, merely because it is extraordinary, merely because it is not part of the ordinary routine service of government, year by year, that it should be in a separate bill. The war was not an ordinary part of the routine service of government year by year, but every war vote came down in the estimates, and over these war votes the Senate had no jurisdiction; but nobody in the Senate complained. Votes of money any government has a right to place in the estimates, and there can 'be no complaint from any quarter.
All that we heard from the government in support of this resolution was a speech somewhat eloquent in the matter of vituperation, but exceedingly vacant in the matter of argument for the measure. I have not heard a suggestion of argument behind the resolution from any member of the government save one.
Does the hon. gentleman state that the war votes all came down in the estimates?
Yes.

I remember distinctly the first session I was in parliament, in' 1918, Sir Robert Borden introduced a resolution dealing with an amount of $500,000,000, and that resolution went through in five minutes. That amount was not in the estimates.
There is always a resolution preceding an estimate.
No.

Why, of course. The
Supply bill is anteceded by a resolution.
This was a special amount.
Was there a bill for it?
I do not remember.
Every war vote was in the estimates.
I beg your pardon, no.

I recommend the hon.
gentleman to look back and improve his historical knowledge, and I am sure he will not come back here and say I was wrong.
I have heard only one contention put forward; it is first of all submitted by the Acting Minister of Finance, and then by the Prime Minister. They say:	The committee
of parliament reported here, and the report was accepted unanimously, that the depositors had a moral claim in equity. Neither of them will say that he believes the depositors have a moral claim in equity. You cannot pry it out of them. I tried with the acting minister, and failed. But they hold in such a secrosanct position the report of a committee of parliament, adopted on a motion without notice, that they are bound in their duty to the country to come forward with a measure of compensation. When did this great sanctity first appertain to a report of a committee accepted by parliament? The Acting Minister of Finance not more than a week ago had to face a report of a committee accepted by parliament, and he did not bring in a measure to implement it, he brought in a measure distinctly to the contrary, and he supported it in this House. What becomes' now of the only argument he seeks to advance behind1 this resolution? In the other case, not only was there one of these acceptances which this government has loosely permitted to follow one after the other against the protests of some of their own friends, against my protest repeatedly and that of other hon. members- in that case not only was there one of these hasty, loose, and ill-considered acceptances, but a minister of the crown rose and distinctly affirmed the government's adherence to the report with one exception, and the government brought in no measure to implement that report, with that one exception- none whatever. So the government is in the position of presenting now a policy, and declining to give any reason behind the policy at all, any reason that they have ever paid a whit of attention to in other days.
Now I do not think there is any disposition on the part of any member of this House in any section to decline to deal fairly, yes more, to decline to deal generously with those who suffer in Canada from no fault of their own, with those who may be in need. These bank depositors are in that class, a great many of them; from what I can learn, the great body
Home Bank

of them are, and if a measure could be brought down-I am not going to stand here just because I am in opposition and say it is a simple thing to do it; I know it is a very difficult thing to do it-but if a measure could be brought down to bring something in the way of relief to those who suffered from that scourge, I do not know that there would be anybody in the House inclined to oppose it. But the government has brought in a measure distinctly on the basis of compensation, and you cannot justify compensation in the absence of an established liability. I do not think any government ever introduced or tried to introduce a measure before in the form of a compensation measure to losers in an investment or losers by way of deposits, unless they did claim to support it, and tried to support it, and succeeded in supporting it on the basis of a liability.
The liability may be of two kinds. I am not one of those who say you cannot have a moral claim. My hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) is strictly right in saying there is no such thing as a moral claim in equity. But there is a moral claim aside altogether from the legal rules of equity You may have a legal claim on which you can sue and recover in a court of law, but you may have a claim you could not recover at all in a court of law, but which has a moral basis, giving the right of collection. Those have occurred many a time. There may be technical obstacles in the way that would prevent recovery in law, but if the moral claim is there, the liability is there which an honourable man will always meet, and which an honourable government always ought to meet. So I say the responsibility may be one of the two kinds; it cannot be of any other kind.
Now the government say: "These people came to us. It was not relief they were asking; they wanted compensation, and they based their claim on one of two grounds, or both: they said, 'In the first place, assuming that on the complaint of 1916 Sir Thomas White did right in declining to wreck the bank, the reason he was right was because there was a war; we should not suffer from the war; therefore we should be paid. Our other contention is this: Sir Thomas White did wrong, he was guilty of negligence or gross error, error of some kind in his conduct, and if he was guilty of error, we should not suffer, we should be paid'." Now, I am free to say that if the depositors could establish either one of those positions, it matters not which, I would think they were entitled to compensation. I do not agree with the hon. member 
to my left from Glengarry and Stormont (Mr. Kennedy), who says that the taxpayers should not pay for the errors of government. I am afraid that that is the responsibility of taxpayers always. If a government errs, representing the taxpayers, the taxpayers have to suffer. They have recourse against the government, or against the individual perhaps; but I do believe it is best that in the case of an error of government-I do not mean an error in discretion, nor an error in judgment, I mean error amounting to negligence or breach of duty-if certain individuals suffer because of an error which amounts to negligence or breach of duty, then I think the treasury should pay.	[DOT]
Now then, did the depositors establish either position? I wish I could submit myself to a jury composed of the hon. Acting Minister of Finance when I put that question to him. Did they establish either position? The Prime Minister says, "We did not like to decide these two contentions. Here we were asked really to pass on the conduct or misconduct of a political opponent; we would not do it. We submitted it to Mr. Justice McKeown." Before Mr. Justice McKeown the depositors came. Did they establish, first, breach of duty on the part oif Sir Thomas Whre? There is not a member of this House who will rise in his place and say so. Mr. Justice McKeown did not find it; not a line of his report would indicate that anything of the kind was established in his mind; not a line. Did they establish that Sir Thomas White would or should have acted otherwise had there not been a war? Again I appeal to the finding of Mr. Justice McKeown. He finds no such thing. He finds, of course, as anybody would find, that what Sir Thomas White did was doubly justified. Because of the conditions that surrounded him, conditions of war, Mr. Justice McKeown finds in effect that what would have been unwise under ordinary circumstances would have been madness in time of war. But he does not find that if there had been no war at all Sir Thomas White should have dene differently from what he did. If he had so found in the face of the evidence, I would stand here and argue definitely to the contrary, for there was not a whit or ti tle of evidence to support any such finding. I am not called upon to do so; the finding is not there.
Then what happens? Still endeavouring to avoid the responsibility which was on the government from the beginning, still endeavouring to postpone, still in the old course of vacillation, they refer the matter to a committee of this House, and the committee brings in a

Home Bank
report with those words, whatever they mean, "that there is a moral claim in equity." Then with no notice whatever, someone gets up and moves the adoption of the report, the Speaker says "carried," and the government, without declaring there is any moral claim at all, without setting their seal on the assertion that there is any moral claim whatever, say, "Because of the acceptance of that report we have got to bring in this measure." Is that reason, is that common sense? If the government had early in the day-because they had every reason then to know there was no breach of duty, they had every reason then to know there was no claim in equity whatever, that all that cculd be asked was a compassionate allowance-if the government had come in with a vote for a compasion-ate allowance, that vote would have carried in this parliament with very, very little objection. I should like to think there would have been no objection whatever from any quarter. It is more difficult to make a compassionate allowance now than a year or so ago. A compassionate allowance should be on a generous scale, but it ought to be on the principle of relief, just as in the case of any scourge or havoc that parliament is disposed to relieve. That is the view I take of this measure. I speak in my individual capacity. I frankly say that with these views I am sorry I cannot express the opinions of all hon. members behind me.

Before my right hon.
friend takes his seat,-probably I did not understand him, but is it not a fact that the relief for the Farmers' Bank was introduced by way of a bill?
It was.

I find by Hansard of
June 2, 1914, that Hon. Sir Thomas White moved the second reading of Bill No. 185, for the relief of the depositors of the Farmers' Bank of 'Canada. Probably I misunderstood my right hon. friend.

No, I have not made my criticism, on that ground at all. I say there is a very great difference of opinion on the subject. There is much to be said for a special bill in such a case. That is all. But I would refrain from making a violent personal attack upon one absent because he differs from me on the point. I hope to that extent I will be supported by the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell). Now, I had really closed what I had to say. I have spoken for myself. I have reasoned it out as carefully as I can. I know in this regard there are thousands-yes,
I think I may say tens of thousands-of people in this country, some of whom can afford it, some of whom have no claim on the treasury whatever, but many of whom cannot, many of whom have lost the earnings of a lifetime, in the failure of this blank. I think the depositors are in a stronger position than any other class. But I must say this, that, acting on the principle of relief, there are many besides the depositors who are entitled to something. Here is a case where the double liability works a cruel, bitter hardship. Think of eleven hundred farmers in the west-not the poorest, for these have no money to put into bank stock; nevertheless some who had money when they put it in, aside from what they have lost on account of the Home Bank, would have nothing now anyway on account of the character of the years that have intervened-think of those men not only losing all they put up, which represents a portion of their savings, but being called upon now, many of them with nothing left, to put up double liability, and then being called upon by the country to contribute to compensation for perhaps scores of men who are wealthy and do not need it at all. I would myself be very charitable to any measure that aimed at the nearest approximation to relief that you can get. I opened by admitting the difficulty of framing a measure not subject to pretty severe criticism in detail aimed at relieving these people; but I would say that if the government had perhaps associated with the liquidator certain men of proved standing in Canada, and made a grant to those men on certain basic principles, namely, defining where relief should be paid, they could have done just the same as a committee in the case of a great fire or a great deluge, they could have distributed that relief to those who needed it most. It would be more difficult than in the cases I have mentioned, but I do not think it would be impracticable, and I do not know of any other principle on which we can possibly assist these people without establishing a precedent and creating gross injustice that we never in the world afterwards can follow and never defend.	.
Now, there is an amendment before the House. I can understand the position of those hon. members who say, "We are not acquainted with the circumstances of the Farmers' Bank, we were not here when those circumstances were disclosed in parliament, we are not familiar with the claims of the Farmers' Bank depositors, and we do not like therefore to support this amendment." I am not in that position; I know the circumstances of the Farmers' Bank claims. I think, on moral grounds, they
Home Bank

are in a far stronger position than the Home Bank depositors. In the case of the Farmers' Bank the dispute arose as to the propriety of the issue of the certificate. Here there is no such dispute, so far as I understand the case; there is dispute as to the wisdom of or the discretion used by the minister in issuing it. In the Farmers' Bank case it was established to the satisfaction of the government and to the satisfaction of the commissioner, Chief Justice Meredith, who investigated, that the moneys which under the law should have been deposited before the certificates issued were really not deposited and therefore that the certificate should not have been issued. He did not charge bad faith against the minister, but he did charge that there was a breach of the regulations, a breach of the law as laid down by parliament in the issue of the certificate itself. I do not think that the weakness of the minister's position in issuing the certificate was the real cause of the failure of the bank. I do not think it was the proximate cause of the loss. If it had been, there would have been a legal claim. But still it is true that if the certificate had only issued as it should have issued then those men would not have lost. On that account we thought there was a moral claim against the state and we brought in a bill accordingly. We thought it was a moral claim and that the depositors were therefore put in just the same position as if they had a legal claim', consequently we paid. In this case there is no contention-there is certainly nothing established to bring it home-that there was breach of duty, breach of regulations, breach of law -none whatever. There is nothing to establish negligence; nothing whatever. All that we can urge upon each other in frankness is that because of the disaster thousands who were not responsible were placed in a position of great distress, commanding the sympathy and deserving the relief, if possible, of the parliament of Canada.

The right hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) states that he is mot in favour of the depositors being reimbursed on a pro rata basis according to their loses; that their cases should be investigated and paid according to the need. A feiw days ago when we were discussing the problem of the revaluation of the assets of soldier settlers, my right hon. friend took the view that all the soldiers should be paid on a percentage basis.

It was not a case of
relief at all.
Absolutely.
Oh, no.

The right hon. gentleman was willing that even the seven hundred odd who were able to pay up their claims in full in one or two years should be given the same percentage of discount as those others whose property had not been fairly appraised.

The hon. member fails
to see this: in the case of the soldiers there was no scourge, no disaster, no collapse.
There was disaster.

No, no; it was just a
case of whether or not the whole soldier body had laboured under difficulties that were too great by reason of the contingencies of the time, that is all. Certainly all of them should be treated alike. You could not distinguish between the fellow who had worked hard and the fellow who had not.

The right hon. gentleman said he thought most of these valuators were honest men, and I agree with that. But there were occasional ones who were not true to their trust, and they stuck the soldiers unmercifully. These victims had a right to consideration, and my right hon. friend said that they should be treated on the same basis as those who had got a good deal from the government.

The hon. member is on
another subject altogether. There was nothing in that case that hinged on the ill-treatment of the soldier by any settlement board. If there was, every single one should be compensated in full. But that was not the case. It was a question of giving general relief because of the fact that generally or over the whole body they had paid too much for stock or for land, owing to the high prices of the time. That is a very different thing from this.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock the resolution to provide compensation for the depositors of the Home Bank was being considered. There is also an amendment by the hon. member for Glengarry and Stormont (Mr. Kennedy) to include in that resolution compensation for the depositors of the old

Home Bank
defunct Farmers' Bank, on whose behalf a bill had been introduced in parliament in 1914 which at that time passed the House of Commons by a substantial majority but was later defeated in the Senate. Since that time many things have happened, and I think that I am safe in saying that banking in Canada is much better understood by the people to-day than it was then. I believe I am also well within the mark in saying that the functions and lack of responsibility of the Canadian Bankers' Association are also' much better understood. I might also make some further observations with regard to other changes that have taken place. One would be that the term "responsible government" in Canada is more of a misnomer to-day than it U9ed to be. Parliament is now asked to vote $5,450,000 of the people's money to certain preferred creditors of the defunct Home Bank of Canada. It is all very well for people to be generous with what belongs to themselves. It is a very laudable thing to see the spirit of generosity actuating people in their private affairs; but I do not consider that the same can be said of those who are disposing of other peoples property without their consent. And to my mind that is the case in the present instance. I do not think the government have offered sufficient justification for the voting of this money. If it was a matter of granting relief instead of compensation the case would be quite different. I was much impressed by the attitude of the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) who refused to admit that the depositors of the Home Bank had even a moral claim, let alone a legal one, for compensation. This being the case I think we should be very careful indeed as to what we are doing under the present circumstances with the resources of this country. I have so expressed myself on several occasions during the present session, and I have urged upon the government the need for the strictest economy and retrenchment in conducting the affairs of Canada. I am sorry to say that there is not any disposition to cut down expenditures, but on the contrary there is the most lavish voting of money regardless of conditions and consequences. I noticed an editorial in the Ottawa Journal of February 19, 1905, which refers to a statement made by a supporter of the government in his own constituency some time previously. The editorial says:
When Mr. "Tim" Healy of Belle River fame told his constituents some weeks ago that Home Bank depositors would be compensated, we said that the statement was sinister. I
I am not going to read the whole of the editorial. It goes on to say:
No more brazen, no more palpable, no more iniquitous election trick has been perpetrated on this country of electioneering afflictions within our memory.
The editorial goes on to point out the injustice of voting money in this particular case, and makes a comparison between two people styled "A" and "B":
"A" and "B" are neighbours. "A" puts his money into the Home Bank. "B" puts his into a factory. A year later "A's" Home Bank collapses, and so does "B's" factory- they both lose. What moral, legal or other right has "A" to come to "B" and say: "You lost and I lost; but I am going to see that you are taxed and made to lose more so that my loss is retrieved".
I think this puts the situation very tersely and exactly as it is. I do not consider there is any more justification or anything like as much justification, for voting this money as there was in several other instances of bank failures which I might mention. I have a very vivid recollection of the debate which took place in this House when the bill to compensate the Farmers' Bank depositors was before parliament in the year 1914. At that time it was very clearly shown, in the case of the Farmers' Bank, that the license or charter was issued under circumstances for which the government were to blame; and it is a most significant thing that the charter for the Home Bank was issued in the same year in which the other was issued but not under anything like as questionable circumstances as in the case of the Farmers' Bank. And in the case of the Farmers' Bank the depositors did not recover anything; they lost the full amount which they had on deposit in that bank at that time. Indeed, many of them were absolutely ruined, and many died as a result of the hardships which had come upon them in their old age through the failure of that bank. Yet in the case of the Farmers' Bank no compensation whatever was granted. In the case of the Home Bank there has 'been quite a substantial surplus saved from the proceeds of the bank; and I think that evidence which has been adduced here this afternoon goes to show that there is some force in the contention that had proper steps been taken by the government and by the Bankers' Association it is quite possible that the Home Bank might not have been forced to go under. I think there is a heavy responsibility upon the government, and also upon the Bankers' Association, for the failure of the Home Bank.
I did not intend to discuss this matter had it not been for the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Glengarry and Stormont. To my mind if there is any justification at all for voting the people's money in such cases, the justification
Home Bank

is twice as strong ini connection with the amendment in the case of the [Farmers' Bank depositors as it is in connection with the original motion relating to the Home Bank depositors. I am sorry the government have not given an assurance that some compensation would be given where there were equally strong, if not stronger, grounds for compensation, as it is termed by the present government. I notice the resolution contains these words:
