That it is expedient to provide for the payment out of the consolidated revenue fund of the sum of $5,450,000.
This word "expedient" is rather significant. The Prime Minister recommended that the government take action by reason of the report which had been made by the commission which had been appointed to investigate this matter. The commission, as was pointed out by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), did not say that there was a legal or a moral claim. Nothing of the kind can be adduced from the report of the commission, but it was a most remarkable statement which the Prime Minister made that if this amendment was tacked on to the resolution it would meet, in all probability the same fate, or the two of them would meet the same fate, in the upper house which the Farmers Bank bill met in 1914. The Prime Minister also made a most remarkable statement with regard to a letter which the acting leader of the Conservative party in the upper house, Senator Robertson, wrote to the chairman of the committee which had been, appointed to look after the interests of the depositors of the Home Bank, and said that he considered the statement contained in this letter to be a distinct threat that if the government undertook to introduce this question by way of a resolution or bill, instead of placing an item in the estimates, the same action would be taken in the Senate. After listening to the statement made, and after carefully following the Prime Minister while he was reading the letter, I could not see that -the letter bore out the statement made by the Prime Minister, and I think that was the opinion of everyone who listened to the reading of the letter. When this view was made evident by hon. members on this side of the House, the Prime Minister became even more emphatic in his statement that in this letter a threat had been madte by the acting leader in the Senate in connection with that matter, and he said: "I think it is a most extraordinary thing that a leader of the Conservative party in the Senate should make the statement to the Home Bank depositors that if any measure came before the Senate with respect to the Home Bank failure, it was

going to be killed in the Senate." I do not think any other hon. member of this House will draw any such deduction from the statements contained in Senator Robertson's letter. It surely shows the desperate straits the government are in when they, at this late stage, after years of pressure having been brought to bear on them to do something, as has 'been pointed out in numerous editorials in the newspapers, right on the verge of an appeal on the country, take action to meet this pressure. I think it is a most unusual course for any government- to take and one which I do not consider reflects any credit upon them. I may say that if it were a matter of relief, it ought to be based upon more substantial grounds than those so far presented as a justification for paying out this money. If this resolution passes, payment will be made to many people who are not in distressed circumstances. Many of them -would not feel their loss very much, if at all.	It is true
there are many cases where people have lost their all, many aged people, and many poor people who have suffered1 greatly in consequence of the failure of this bank. I am sure that if we had had a little more insight into the failure of the Home Bank before the last revision of the Bank Act was passed some changes would have been made to place greater responsibility upon the Bankers' Association in regard to such matters.
The only feature of the motion before the House which meets with my approval is that contained in the amendment which provides a small meed of compensation to those who lost their all through- the failure of the Farmers Bank a number of years ago, and who did not receive one dollar out of the wreck of the bank. No redress has been provided for them, and in this case those who have suffered through the Home Bank failure are to receive a considerable amount, and will in all probability lose about sixty-five cents on the dollar. It is a hardship I admit, and they are entitled to great sympathy, but we are not here to exercise sympathy, we are here to do business for the people, to -protect the resources of this country and not to use those resources for anything except legitimate purposes.
Mr. ST. PERE (Translation): Mr. Chairman, I rise for the second time in the House to plead on behalf of the depositors of the Home Bank. The latter petitioned the Government, last year, in order to obtain assistance and brought to bear the following reasons so as to well establish their request.
Protests were made to the Minister of Finance, in 1916 and 1918, in connection with the

Home Bank
critical state in which the Home Bank found itself at that time. If, as the petitioners contend, an enquiry had been instituted, as provided by section 56A of the Bank Act, the actual situation in which the Home Bank found itself at that time would have certainly been shown, and this institution would have been put in liquidation or merged with another bank. In either case, the depositors would not have lost their money. Moreover, twenty-seven or twenty-eight new branches would not subsequently have been opened, and this would have avoided losses to new depositors. In the report of the royal commission appointed by the present government, the Hon. Chief Justice McKeown states that, if the bank had closed its doors in 1916 or 1918, all of the depositors' money would have been safeguarded.
Sir Thomas White, then Minister of Finance, stated in giving evidence, that he did not dare to place the bank in liquidation, owing to the war and that such a step on his part might have prejudiced the financial stability of Canada. The following are Sir Thomas White's words:
It you make a mistake in putting in an auditor in peace time the consequences may be a run producing little effect upon the bank; if in war time, you may bring down the bank and, in addition, you may cause an unspeakable calamity to the country.
It is evidently this last consideration which prompted the Minister of Finance to act as he did.
The report of the Royal Commission was submitted to the Banking and Commerce committee, at the last session of Parliament, and the committee, in its report to the House, stated that the depositors have a moral right in equity to a compensation.
This report of the committee on Banking and Commerce was unanimously adopted by the House at its last session. Consequently, the Parliament of Canada, in plenary meeting, recognized and decreed that the depositors of the Home Bank have a moral right and claim in equity to relief. It is useless to quibble or evade the question so as to minimize the facts which are all very conclusive. The 60,000 depositors of the Home Bank, who represent about 400,000 people anxiously expect that this unanimous vote of parliament will take the more concrete form of dollars and cents, and they feel more and more confident in regard to promises made by the government.
The failure of the Home Bank is not simply a provincial or civic question which the Dominion government can set aside. It was so to speak a national disaster which affected
60,000	depositors or about 400.000 people
residing between the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. It has cast its shadow over a great number of families that have been ruined; a large number of people, owing to the trust they placed in the stability of the chartered banks of the Dominion, have lost all their savings by depositing them in the Home Bank and a great number of children owing to this fact have been deprived of the means which would have provided for their future. And moreover this failure has been the cause of many deaths and a number of suicides; it is with regret that such things must be referred to.
The Home Bank depositors do not appeal to sympathy or charity to support their claim, but they rely upon the justice of their cause, as it has been clearly shown in the report of the committee on Banking and Commerce presented to parliament, at the last session, and in which it is stated and asserted that they have a moral claim in equity to being reimbursed. The facts of the case speak for themselves. Could the depositors, in fact, ever bring forward a claim which would rest on more solid grounds than the moral law of equity and right? The moral law is at the very basis of all legislation of the British Empire, and is superior to all other forms of jurisprudence. It is, indeed, from the moral standpoint that all laws, provincial or federal obtain ;heir force and sanction. It is claimed that the depositors have no legal right to a reimbursement, and this, because it is a principle of the English law "that the King and his government can do no wrong." Some legislators have contended that to reimburse the depositors of the Home Bank would create a dangerous precedent which would open the door to further claims, if other financial institutions were to have the same fate as the Home Bank. This argument cannot hold, owing to the recent amendments made to the Bank Act. There, however, exists precedents, as governments have come to the assistance of unfortunate depositors, not only in England, but also in Canada. It is but necessary to recall the McGriggor Bank affair, in England, and that of the Upper Canada Bank in our own country, and more recently still, the stand taken by the legislature of the province of Quebec, in guaranteeing the emission of a large amount of debentures in favour of the Hochelaga Bank, to avoid the disaster which the failure of the Banque Nationale might have brought on, in 1924. It is but necessary to consider these recent precedents to admit the fairness of the popular legislation

Home Bank

that the present government is introducing to assist the unfortunate depositors of the Home Bank.
Objection might perhaps be raised that the attitude taken in 1916 and 1918 by the exMinister of Finance Sir Thomas White, places no responsibility on the present ministers of the Mackenzie King government, and that the Liberal government of to-day, cannot be held1 responsible for the blunders committed by the late government. We feel certain that our legislators will consider the claims of the Home Bank depositors with a more open mind and a fairer view of the matter. All governments assume the duties, responsibilities and obligations of the administrations to which they succeed. Their joint liability is in no way put in doubt on such a question.
Equity, it is stated, is law in fhe present case. This moral obligation is, so to speak, the law which must protect the injured rights of the depositors; it further places the hon. members of this House, in the most favourable situation to freely and easily carry out their duty and thus realize, to the (best of their ability, the ideal of the rights of the people. The existence itself of society is inconceivable, notwithstanding the wisdom and strength of its institutions, if it does not show a certain amount of good faith, equity and fortitude. The depositors have always acted in good faith, therefore let us have the courage, to-day, to treat them with equity. Let us not fear to create a precedent, for all legislation, which basis its principles and existence on moral law and equity, becomes, for the country which accepts it, an efficient protection and the indispensable condition of its development.
Therefore, Sir, I shall vote against the amendment and in favour of the resolution.

When the resolution was
under discussion this afternoon I was not in the House, and consequently I have been informed only within the past half hour of the discussion that took place then. I do not intend to express an opinion as to the merits or demerits of the resolution which has been introduced into the House by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). It would, I feel, be inappropriate for me to take any part in that discussion because of the relations which, for a number of years, I had with the Home Bank in the capacity of a director. The story of the failure of the Home Bank is fully before the public in the report of the Mc-Keown commission of inquiry a year ago and in the various cases that have been before the courts. I do not know that anything can 
be added by way of information to the committee that is not already in public evidence.
The ex-Minister of Finance, the hon. member for West York, (Sir Henry Drayton), if the information I have received in respect to his remarks this afternoon is accurate, he left the impression very clearly in the minds of the committee that Sir Thomas White, who was Minister of Finance in 1916, had stayed his hand as regards an inquiry into the position of the bank on account of certain representations which I had made to him. In this the hon. member has scarcely done me justice or, perhaps, he has done me a little more than justice, because I am very certain that any statement which I may have made to Sir Thomas White was only a factor, a relatively unimportant factor for that matter, in causing him to reach any decision that he did reach as to the course which he should pursue.
It may not be out of place, since the matter has been brought up-and I think it is only just to myself and to those who have been associated with me that I should deal with it-* to say that the western directors of whom I was one, along with two others in the city of Winnipeg, were an advisory committee in western Canadla to deal with the western business of the Home Bank. Other banks have such committees, and during the whole period from the time that I became a member of the board, I think in 1910, to the end of 1914, I attended only one directors' meeting in Toronto which happened to be on a date when I was in that city. In the latter part of 1914, information reached us-and the particulars of this are set out in my evidence before the McKeown commission-thait things were not as well as they should be in the head office of the bank. We were then into the war. We had been in it for several months. My colleagues and I appreciated our responsibility as directors, and for that purpose we came to Toronto and asked for certain information. It is always a painful and a very difficult thing to speak words that, even by implication may criticize a man who has died and who is not here to defend himself, and I wish to be as careful as I can in any statement I make in that respect. But I am compelled to say that we found things were not as they should have been. We found that the board of directors had not been informed; in fact, I may go further and say that the board of directors had been misinformed by the eastern management. I think that came as a painful surprise to our fellow directors in eastern Canada, men of high business repute in the city of Toronto. What we sought to achieve then was a better management. We were unable to secure that. I do not wish

Home Bank
to criticize my fellow directors at that time in eastern Canada, but we could not get their support then to a change in management which the western directors wished to make, and it was that condition which led us, in view of the circumstance that Canada was in the war and the serious responsibility that rested upon us as directors, to come to the conclusion, under, I may say, the best legal advice we could get at that date, that our clear duty was to lay the facts before the then Minister of Finance. That we did. When that action was taken, the Minister of Finance of the day, Sir Thomas White, took the matter up at once with the officials of the bank, and then and not until then were we able to displace the management which, in our judgment, should have been displaced a year before. I quite appreciate that the representations which we made to the Minister of Finance were of a serious character. We did not take that action-and I am sure Sir Thomas White would be the last one in Canada to say that we had so done it-in any way to make difficulties for him. But when information came before the Minister of Finance, he asked for certain details of the business. On the advice of the western directors, on their suggestion and, I may say, at their urging, Mr.. Z. A. Lash, whose reputation as a business man and as a banker none in this House or outside of it will gainsay, was appointed as counsel for the bank. It was represented by Sir Thomas White that he thought he should send someone from the outside to inquire into the position of the bank. At that time the eastern directors, Mr. Lash and the management of the bank unreservedly and unquestionably took the view that any such action might precipitate a crisis in the bank's affairs. They urged that an examiner could not be sent in from outside to inquire into the business of the bank without that news getting on the street and having its reaction on depositors, and the bank perhaps being forced to close its doors. Now that opinion may have been right or it may have been wrong. I am simply giving the committee what the opinion was at that time, and on the strength of this opinion, and at the request of Mr. Lash, I wrote to Sir Thomas White a letter which I understand my hon. friend from West York quoted this afternoon. In that letter I pointed out that the old management had been displaced, that Mr. Haney in whom Mr. Lash and other eastern directors had a great deal of confidence was going to take more active charge of the 254i
bank's affairs, that Mr. MeHaffie of the Winnipeg office, a trained banker, was coming to Toronto to assist Mr. Haney, and that I felt under the circumstances the information we desired could be secured from within instead of sending in someone from without, and "that at this juncture"-I have not seen that letter for a year, but I am very sure that my hon. friend from West York will find those words in it-"that at this juncture it is better for the inquiry to proceed from within than without."

That is about
correct. The hon. member said:
In my opinion the situation has materially improved within the last month, and at this juncture, with the changes in management recently made, it is better to have the inquiry proceed from within than without.

That was the view I took. I thought there was a distinct improvement, and I still think so, owing to the fact that we had displaced the old management. Let ine repeat again, where I think my hon. friend from West York has scarcely been just to me is that he left the impression on the minds of the committee, if the information I got is correct, that Sir Thomas White stayed bis hand only because of the representations I had made to him. Now those representations were only a part of the thing, and perhaps a minor part, in what influenced Sir Thomas White in the position he took. I feel this, and I say it now: I feel Sir Thomas White was quite warranted in relying, for instance, upon the opinion of Mr. Z. A. Lash, because Mr. Lash was not only a very able business man but also an able banker.
I understand that some criticism has been levelled against Sir Thomas White this afternoon. If there has been, I wish to dissociate myself entirely from it. I have no reason to think other than that Sir Thomas White acted in what in his judgment was the best interests of the country. It may be there was an error of judgment; I am not prepared even to say that, viewing the circumstances as they were at that time, because the course then taken has to be judged in the light of the facts then existing; it cannot be judged in the light of facts that may have been disclosed seven or eight years later. Consequently I simply wish to say that I dissociate myself entirely from any criticism of Sir Thomas White in that respect.
The whole episode of the failure of the bank was a deplorable thing, but I still think that if a vigorous management had taken hold of the bank at that time, at any rate the tremendous failure and loss that finally resulted would not have taken place. That
Home Bank

was.the judgment of Sir Thomas White then; it was my judgment then, and it is my judgment now, and I care not who in this country knows it.
I do not know that I have anything further to add. It is a regrettable thing that in our political discussions sometimes in this House and often in the country we deal more in personalities than in principles. Such a thing is not elevating to the public life of the country. I am not criticizing the government for the action it has taken. I am neither criticizing nor approving, for the reasons I gave in my opening remarks, but whatever discussion there is in the country or in the House on this matter, I trust may be kept above the level of personalities and the case dealt with entirely on its merits.

I do not intend to take up much of the time of the House with this discussion, but I do want to give a reason why the government should come to the relief of the depositors in this ibanik. The parliament of Canada has a Bank Act, it has one to-day, and this House and the Senate are responsible for it. We give authority to banks to issue their own notes, which are mere promises to pay-il have some of them in my hand now; I
have just been reading them over-"The..bank
will pay to the bearer on demand one or five or ten dollars," that is all there is to it. This has been going on in this country now for forty or fifty years, and it has been the cause of 70 per cent of the bank failures in Canada It has been the ambition of every small bank that has started in this country to get on its feet and get into the business because of that permission to issue their own notes given by the Bank Act to the banks. We have to stop that, or else these failures will continue They will go on as long as we keep the law where it is to-day and give this right to any private company to take out a charter, go into the banking business and issue its own notes, which are only promises to pay on demand one or five or ten dollars, the first day it opens its doors. No one here has dared to face that issue. The Minister of Finance is no more responsible for it than the previous minister, but the parties in this House are responsible for it, and the lesson to-day is not that we ought to come to the relief so much of the Home Bank in this case, as we ought to come to the relief of the public generally, and get what they have got in the United States.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the hon.
gentleman is getting somewhat out of order. This resolution deals with the expediency of

reimbursing the depositors of the Home Bank, and there is an amendment thereto respecting the Farmers' Bank. A general discussion of the Bank Act, currency and so forth, is not in order.
Mr. MACLEAN (York) - If you will pardon me, Mr. Chairman, somebody has suggested, and I knew this argument would be made, that there is no reason why the government should come to the relief of the Home Bank depositors. I say they are bound to come to the relief of the depositors of the bank as long as they allow the law to be as it is, giving the banks in this country the right to issue their own notes; and that is the opinion of the country at large to-day, Mr. Chairman. I would like the Acting Minister of Finance to read a review in the Wall Street Journal of last week dealing with the Canadian banking situation and pointing out all these facts, pointing out this enormous right that the banks in Canada have of issuing their own notes. They have not got it in the United States. The United States today is the greatest banking country in the world, and it is great because all the notes in circulation by the banks of the United States are the notes of the United States, backed by the credit of the whole country. That is why they are the leading bankers of the world to-day, that and the national reserve banking system they have in the United States.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that this is a question of the expediency of reimbursing the Home Bank depositors. Inferentially the hon. member may deal with the Bank Act, but he is not entitled to make a speech on the system of banking in different countries of the world.

It is all right if it is a
good speech.

It is a good speech; and I am the best judge of a good speech. The whole condition of Canada is critical, and if there is one situation more critical than another it is the banking situation. We must cure it, and we will never do so while we hide from ourselves in this House the fact that parliament is responsible for this condition of affairs which has made it necessary for the government to come to the relief of the Home Bank depositors. Under the American system they have what they call member banks in connection with the federal bank, which checks off every bank from time

Home Bank
to time, and if we had 'had that system in effect here the condition of the Home Bank would have been discovered years before and would have been cured. If we continue to say, as we are saying here, "There is no responsibility on parliament to vote this money," I say we are mistaken, I say this parliament is responsible because we created this condition and we must cure it. Therefore I am going to vote for this relief to be granted to the depositors of the Home Bank. I have given reasons why parliament should intervene and do something, not why we should get up here and dig up the records of various parties in connection with the question. We have been side-stepping all afternoon, and the moment I get up and give reasons why parliament should come to the relief of these depositors I am "disciplined" for dealing with the only question at issue. I am leaving the question there with the people, and I am saying to the depositors of the Home Bank, "You ought to be paid because parliament created the banking system that allowed the banks to issue their own notes payable on demand to bearer, instead of creating a better system under which this failure would not have been possible." Now, another issue has come up. Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, you will call m.e to order, but we have been talking a good deal this afternoon about the second chamber. Everybody says that that chamber is the equal of this House, and that we should not speak about it. Yet the Prime Minister has been speaking about it, and he is calling an interprovincial conference to discuss the upper house. I say that so long as it has its present powers that house is our equal. When the people of Canada think-and I believe they do already- that any irresponsible chamber ought not to be continued, but that it should be made responsible by having its membership elected for a definite term, then we shall have a reform of our constitution. The great question in England to-day is the reform of the House of Lords. The great question in Canada to-day is the reform of our constitution. The people think as I do, and will not approve of our attitude that we need not discuss the banking question or the rights of the other house because "there is no reason for doing so." I have discussed these questions on previous occasions, and I think I will have an opportunity of discussing them again. I believe some measures of reform will come. The great reforms that we want are: first, the revision of the Bank Act where I say it is wrong; and, second, reform of the upper chamber so that those who sit there will be responsible to the country, and they will become so when they are elected for a fixed term of office by the people of Canada or b3T the provincial legislatures.
Mr. MoOREA:	It is unfortunate that the
depositors of the Home Bank have lost their money, but they are not the only unfortunate people in this country. Many people have invested their life savings in enterprises more for the purpose of developing the country than of making money, and they have lost their capital. The man who puts his money in a bank does so in order that he may receive a revenue from it without doing any work; but the man who invests his money in industrial and other enterprises very often does so for the purpose of developing the country rather than for the revenue he may make out of it.
This bill which is now before us is an absolutely new departure from anything we have ever attempted in this country. Men have lost their money, as I say, in various enterprises, they have lost their money in banks, they have lost it in other ways, but I have never yet seen the government come to their rescue and make good their losses. I grant everybody would be pleased if there was some way of giving the necessary relief without placing additional burdens on an already very heavily burdened people. I should like every member on both sides of the House to realize the fact that the average bill of taxes on each of our 235 constituencies represents a burden of $10,212,276. Now we are asked, absolutely without any justification as far as my judgment goes, to place a further burden on each constituency of $23,191.50. I would ask every hon. member to think of this before he casts his vote. This further burden may appear light, but nevertheless it is an added burden, and we all know that it was the last straw that broke the camel's back. While I sympathize with the depositors of the Home Bank, I see no reason why they should be entitled to any more consideration than other people who have invested their money, wisely as they thought, and lost it all.
But in my judgment the money feature is not the most serious part of this proposition. It is admitted by everybody whom I have heard express any opinion on the matter, that there is no legal dbligation on the government to reimburse the Home Bank depositors; it is simply a moral obligation. Well, as I understand, a moral obligation is never outlawed. If that be true, then every man who has lost money in bank failures of the last thirty years has just as much reason to come before parliament and ask for reimbursement as the
Home Bank

Home Bank depositors have. If this measure becomes law. I do not understand how this government in the future can refuse to make good any losses that may be sustained by other depositors should any other of our chartered banks fail. In my judgment, the money that will be required to meet this obligation is small compared with the prospective obligations which the government may have to assume at some later date, and therefore I trust and hope that every member, no matter on which side of the House he sits, will think not only of the application of this principle to the present case but also to other cases in the future to which disappointed depositors may claim that it should be made to apply.

Fortunately we are not called upon in the determination of this question to assess the responsibility for the collapse of the Home Bank. If the courts of the land do not assess that responsibility, then -certainly the judgment of history will duly assess it.
I want to say at the outset that the claim of the depositors of the Home Bank is not based upon negligence. The original claim which they made for reimbursement to the Governor General in Council did not suggest negligence on anybody's part, so far as I recall. It is true that one of the counsel for the Home Bank depositors-perhaps in fairness I should mention his name; Mr. Lee- did in the course of the investigation before Chief Justice McKeown suggest that Sir Thomas White had been guilty of negligence; did suggest also negligence on the part of Mr. Fielding; did suggest also, I think, negligence on the part of the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) while he was acting as Minister of Finance. I think these statements were very il'l-advised, and I have the best of authority for suggesting that they were made completely without the authority of the Home Bank Depositors' Association. Not only that, but Chief Justice McKeown, after a very careful investigation, did not find negligence on the part of anyone. More than that, the Banking and Commerce committee's report used these words, indicating that so far as it was concerned there was no suggestion of a finding of negligence:
Your committee is not called upon to question the manner in wh/ich Sir Thomas White made use of the powers given to him, or whether he exercised his discretion correctly or otherwise.
But the claim of the Home Bank depositors has been found by the Banking and Commerce committee to be what was denominated a moral claim in equity. Frankly, an apprecia-	j
tion of the significance of those terms will necessarily present some difficulty. But. there can be no question about this: no one can have a legal claim against the government. No government can be sued without its consent, consequently it is fair to say that the Home Bank depositors would have no legal claim against the government. What claim they might have must be other than a legal claim.
I do not understand the hon. member's reasoning there. Does he say that anybody can have a legal claim against the government?
Well, so far as the government is concerned it certainly cannot be sued without its own consent.

That has nothing at all
to do with the question of the legality of the claim.
If the claim is one that cannot be realized upon, then certainly it is c-f no value to the claimant.

If the fiat is granted,
then it is the legality which is tested; the courts decide whether or not the claimant has a legal claim. The question of granting or not granting a fiat has nothing whatever to dc- with the legality of the claim.

I am suggesting to my right
hon. friend that I am using the term with this significance; unless one gets 9 p.m. the consent of the government to prosecute his claim he is absolutely out of court; under the law he can have no- claim. I am not seeking to justify my words simply by differences which are, perhaps, indefinite distinctions. But I do say, and it is held by the Banking and Commerce committee, that the Home Bank depositors have no legal claim against the government, for reimbursement.
Now, upon what does their claim rest? It seems to me it rests upon two or three very definite particulars. First of all, the attention of the Minister of Finance of the day was called at two different times to the condition of the Home Bank arising out of the situation which then existed. Sir Thomas White did not, feel justified in taking action which but for the war he probably would have taken. I desire to- read, Mr. Chairman, a statement given by Sir Thomas White himself in evidence in this connection. This is taken from page 345 of the evidence:	,
I would never think of putting in a special auditor in a bank and taking chances, especially at a time like that, of closing the bank.

Home Bank
And further he says, page 359:
Under no circumstances would I have allowed a bank to fail during the iperiod in question. I had many difficult and dangerous financial situations to deal with during the war. At its outbreak, in view of the panic which prevailed, the government at my instance placed itself behind the banks of Canada and gave public assurance that it would loan them such sums a3 they might require to meet the conditions of the war, and would take all further steps necessary to safeguard the financial situation during its continuance.
And further:
The action I took was in my discretion; in exercising his discretion, a minister must have regard to conditions, because conditions have a direct bearing upon the consequences attendant on his action to the bank and the general situation. If you make a mistake in putting in an auditor, in peace time the consequences may be a run producing little effect upon the bank; if in war time, you may bring down the bank and, in addition, you may cause an unspeakable calamity to the country.
That is the statement of Sir Thomas White, given in evidence before Chief Justice Mc-Keown. Exercising what seems to me to have been a sound discretion, he decided not to take any action in the premises. Now, that is the situation that existed; that is the reason given by Sir Thomas White for having failed to take action.
One of the questions to which Chief Justice McKeown was requested to answer was as follows:
What effect would an audit under section 56A of the Bank Act, if made in 1915, 1916 and 1918, have had upon the conduct of affairs of the said bank and upon the position of the present depositors?
In answer to this question, he said:
For the reasons above set out, I think an effective audit under section 56A of the Bank Act made in 1916 or 1918, would have resulted, as far as concerns the conduct of the bank's affairs, in either,
(a)	liquidation immediately following such audit, or,
(b)	amalgamation with another bank.
And the effect of such audit upon the position of the present depositors:-
If made in 1916, the present depositors would have suffered no loss.
If made in 1918, I do not think any loss would have fallen upon them.
Taking into consideration the statements of Sir Thomas WThite and the findings of Chief Justice McKeown, it is perfectly clear that but for the war, and if the ordinary action had been taken which might have been expected, the Home Bank depositors would have suffered no loss at all. Owing to the war that action was not taken, and therefore it does seem to me that the Home Bank depositors have laid a basis in equity and in fairness to be compensated to some extent at least by this government.
I notice that it is proposed to pay these depositors thirty-five per cent only of their
claim. If the claim is a proper one; if it is one which should be paid by the government at all, then it seems to me that in logic the only thing is to pay it in full. But in view of the fact that the Home Bank Depositors' Association, representing the thousands of depositors from one end of the country to the other, have indicated their approval of this adjustment, I have no comment, Sir, to make. May I say, however, that I would have preferred if a graduated scale of payments had been used instead of the present proposed method. Such a method it seems to me would not only be preferable, but it would be fairer, it would be juster, and most important of all it would do the greatest possible good to those most deserving. I presume that this matter too has been taken up by the government with the Home Bank Depositors' Association. I do not know, but if it could be worked out-and I think it can be-it would be a far more desirable basis of adjustment to adopt.
I understand that the right hon. leader of the opposition feels that in reimbursing the depositors this parliament is placing an unjust burden upon the shareholders of this defunct bank? They are called upon not only to pay a double liability, but also to pay their share of the taxes levied to make up the reimbursement of the Home Bank depositors. I have been credibly informed, however, that in practically every case the shareholders of this bank are depositors also; consequently the loss will not be as great as it might otherwise appear. More than that the shareholders were represented by counsel at the commission presided over by Mr. Justice McKeown and gave, in effect at least, their approval to reimbursement. I understand they have no objection whatsoever.
There is one other matter that was referred to to which I wish to direct a few remarks. It was suggested that the depositors should get the complete and full benefit of this appropriation. With that I am in full agreement. It was suggested, also, that an arrangement had been made that five per cent of this sum was to be used for the purpose of paying the promoters-shall I say?-of the bill, and that there were legal and other expenses-

I may say right here that
matter was only suggested this afternoon, and if it can be proven we will withdraw the bill.

I trust that no opportunity
will be afforded the minister to withdraw the bill. I am informed, on what I consider the best of authority-because I made inquiry into the matter myself, it is somewhat disturbing

-that the depositors themselves have raised every dollar that has been expended on their behalf; that they have financed the depositors' committee, that they have financed and proposed to finance in full the legal costs and charges that were incurred on their behalf. So that if the representations made to me are correct, and I have no doubt they are, the depositors will get the benefit of every dollar of the money appropriated by this parliament for the purposes of their reimbursement.

The Acting
Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) to-day, following his customary practice, presented this most important matter in a very terse and concise way to the House. He reviewed clearly and distinctly the various Steps that have led up to this resolution. He pointed out that shortly after the failure of the Home Bank, through a process of law, a liquidator was appointed and later on the depositors formed themselves into groups throughout the country

formed what was known- as depositors' committees. These committees, through representatives from individual bodies, finally met in Toronto and there drew up a manifesto which they presented to the government of the day. They claimed at that time that their position as depositors was different from that of depositors of banks that had failed previous to the failure of the Home Bank. They claimed that in the year 1916 and on to 1918, the bank was not in a condition to continue business; that the Minister of Finance of that day was advised of the seriousness of the bank's condition, and that if he had exercised his power he could have directed a special audit of the bank. They did not represent to the government that the Minister of Finance had failed in his duty in not instituting this special audit, but they did represent that in 1916, and on to 1918, the minister did not exercise his power but, in view of the existing situation, allowed the condition that prevailed to go on-that if the audit -had been made the doors of the institution would probably have -closed, and if that had happened there would have been sufficient money to have paid the depositors. That -was the statement made in the representations of the depositors to the government; I am summarizing the circumstances because I do not wish to delay the House.
The government after hearing the representations of the depositors, and they were expressed by skilled counsel, followed the course which governments had usually followed under like circumstances. The Governor in Council appointed a royal commission, and Mr. Justice McKeown was chosen to hold an inquiry and 
bring out the facts and the evidence. That inquiry took place and was carried on over a period of days if not of weeks. Witnesses were examined and Mr. Justice McKeown- I do not believe, as the right hon. leader of the opposition said to-day that the commissioner made a finding-placed the evidence before the government. Then the -government, following the customary and proper procedure, brought the report to parliament by which it was referred to the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce. That committee, in its judgment, referred the matter to a sub-committee originally composed of five members but later on enlarged to seven. That sub-committee was instructed to review the evidence brought out by Mr. Justice McKeown and report back to the general committee. That was the procedure followed up to that date.
The right hon. leader of the opposition this afternoon twitted the Acting Minister of Finance and said that he would not say there was a moral claim, neither would any of the ministers. My right hon. friend, however, forgets that one of the most important committees, of the House-the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce-through its sub-committee did find there was a moral claim in equity. More than that, the general committee adopted the findings of the subcommittee by a large majority. So I do not think we need beat around the bush on the question as to whether there is a moral claim or not. The sub-committee of the Banking and Commerce committee found there was a moral claim in equity. That finding was confirmed by the committee itself, and later by this parliament. Therefore I contend that the resolution before us to-day is founded on the fact that there is a moral claim in- equity. Following that up I will read a short extract from the committee's findings which is to be found in the report of the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce for 1924:
Your committee have sat from time to time, and have studied the interim report on the Home Bank submitted by Mr. Chief Justice McKeown and the evidence therein referred to.
Your committee consider that the facts therein brought out and the evidence therein referred to clearly establish that the depositors of the Home Bank have no claim under the law of the land for compensation by the country on account of any loss they may suffer by reason of the failure of the Home Bank.
But your committee are also of the opinion that, in view of the representations made to the Department of Finance in the years 1916 and 1918, the government of the time could have made in 1916 and in 1918 an effective audit under section 56A of the Bank Act, and if such an effective audit or thorough investigation into the bank's affairs had been made it would have resulted :-

1.	In the immediate liquidation of the bank, or
2. Its amalgamation with another bank, and that the effect would have been, no loss to the depositors in 1916 or 1918.
Your committee have studied the evidence given before the roj'al commission by Sir Thomas White, who was then Minister of Finance, and particularly his statements:	"I would never think of putting in a
special auditor in a bank and taking chances, especially at a time like that, of closing the bank" (page 345);
And further:
"Under no circumstances would I have allowed a bank to fail during the period in question. I had many difficult and dangerous financial situations to deal with during the war. At its outbreak, in view of the panic which prevailed, the government, at my instance, placed itself behind the banks of Canada and gave public assurance that it would loan them such sums as they might require to meet the conditions of the war, and would take all further steps necessary to safeguard the financial situation during its continuance", (page 359).
And further:
"The action I took was in my discretion: in exercising his discretion, a minister must have regards to conditions, because conditions have a direct bearing upon the consequences attendant on his action to the bank and the general situation. If you make a mistake in putting in an auditor, in peace time the consequences may be a run producing little effect upon the bank; if in war time, you may bring down the bank and, in addition, you may cause an unspeakable calamity to the country", (page 743).
Thait was the evidence of iSir Thomas White which they quoted. The report 'continues:
Your committee is not called upon to question the manner in which Sir Thomas White made use of the powers given to him, or wrhether he exercised his discretion correctly or otherwise.
Your committee consider that the facts brought out in the Interim Report submitted by Mr. Chief Justice McKeown, and the evidence therein referred to, establish that the depositors of the Home Bank have a moral claim in equity for compensation by the country on account of any loss they may suffer by reason of the failure of the Home Bank.
I W'iilll not read the concluding paragraph of the report, because it was struck out on a motion by one of the members, 'but the question being put on the main motion for the adoption of the report, it was agreed to in the affirmative, yeas 27 and nays, 11, and the chairman ordered the presentation of the report as agreed to by this committee.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not think if one takes into consideration the committee's report, and1 the fialct that this report was adapted by the House, that there can be any question in 'the imind of any 'hon. gentleman in this House that there is a moral claim established here. My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition said that he would agree to a compassionate 'allowance. Personally I do not think this is a case for a compassionate allowance. The claim has been established and payment should be made in a proper way.
Would the minister please give us his interpretation of a moral claim in equity?
I do not require to give it.
I do not think the minister can, but I would like to hear him try.

This is a claim made by the depositors, many of whom lost their all in the unfortunate occurrences that took place during the years 1916 to 1918. Without laying any blame at the door of anyone, there were conditions existing in the country that did create moral claims, and many moral claims have been assented to by this government. As far as the constituency I have the honour to represent is concerned,
I know the people resident there. Many of them come from the eastern provinces, from the Maritimes, many of them come from the Old Country, Scotland and Wales and many of them from the continent of Europe. I have had close associations with these -people over a number of years, and they are not the type of people who appeal for compassionate allowances. I have seen them under great trials and tribulations. I was in the city of Fernie following the explosion where one hundred of the husbands and sons of the mining people had been killed in one blast. I have seen them when fire destroyed their homes, practically wiping out the city completely, so that they were required to move out for a period. I have seen them also during the periods of epidemics, when there was sickness in every household and death at their doors. I refer to the epidemic of 1918. I know the fortitude of these people and I know that they accepted the situation on every occasion as something beyond their control, but they met it standing up. When I visited the city of Fernie on New Year's day in 1924 I found a body of men and women of an entirely different mind and disposition from that which they possessed under other trials and tribulations.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that this is one case probably in the history of this country when we can take a different view without establishing a precedent, because I hope in our time and generation we will never have conditions existing in Canada such as we experienced during the war period where it was necessary for ministers, on account of the war and conditions then existing, to do probably what they would not have done under normal conditions. Later on, it was stated in the House that Sir Thomas White did not wish to take action owing to the war. We have committed so many blunders since 1914; under the plea of war! I did not think that this government or any of its members would dare one day make use of the war as a mantle to cover their deeds! Indeed, I thought that all this ended with the general elections of 1921.

Now, Sir, are we in a position to undertake all this expenditure, such as $5,450,000 and other five millions-it .is always a case of five million dollars? I am wondering where all this will lead us to. I somewhat share the views of my hon. friend from Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea): Where shall we find the money? Borrow 1
In the past, we had in the county of La-prairie and Napiervdlie, three bank failures; not one, but three: the Ville-M-arte Bank, the Banque du Peuple and the Banque de Saint-Jean. There happened to be in my county, three branches of 'the Banque de Saint-Jean and we received from the liquidator of the latter bank, at the end of two years, thirty cents on the dollar, and from the liquidator of the Ville-Maiie Bank, eleven cents on the dollar. Did the government of that day think of reimbursing us? No.
When the question of the Farmers' Bank was being discussed by the House, in 1913, I had occasion of taking part in the debate, and I well remember what I suggested -then to my good friend Mr. Henderson, who was one of the oldest members of the House: If you will undertake to indemnify the depositors of the three -banks that failed in my part of -the country, I shall support your request ion behalf of the Farmers' Bank. Is the government -going to be so unfair, Mr. Chairman, -on the eve of going before the people? 1 cannot conceive -it.
We are told that Sir Thomas White -would not take -action at the -time, because it was during the war; but the war ended in 1918, on November 11, through the -armistice. If 'he were sincere, why did he -not take action -after the war? Why did he not call a meeting of this corrupt Board of directors-for when -a bank fails, it is because the management is corrupt? They are thieves, brigands. Why should the country pay for this failure? No, this is not the way to carry on business. I aim -more -than tired of this kind of -thing. If Sir Thomas White was so much in earnest in 1916 and 1918, why was he -not so after the war? He could have Closed -the doors of that institution after November 11, 1918. I would very much like to know what was the -amount

Could not the ex-Miinister of Finance t the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayition) have also done something when he succeeded to Sir Thomas White? In the first instance, I wish to. congratulate the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) on the statement he made this evening. It was a fair statement and it does not conflict with a single word that I said that I can recollect. My statement was, as I think he learned, occasioned by what I considered to be a most uncalled-for attack upon Sir Thomas White by a former follower of the hon. member for Marquette in connection with an action which Sir Thomas White took, certainly upon the advice and at the request of the hon. member for Marquette, If the hon. member for Marquette will take the trouble to look at Hansard to-morrow, I think he will find that not only did I give him credit for honesty in his representations, but I continued that credit for honesty right down to the end of this whole transaction with the bank, yes, right down to the time when 'he sold his last share. I was pleased to do that as I thought it was right, as I thought it was true. In connection with the claim, the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) has not helped me very much as
to what a moral claim in equity is. From his definition, I take it that it would be any claim against the government, no matter what that claim rested upon, that had not been fortified by a fiat. In other words, a moral claim becomes a legal claim against a government when a fiat has been granted.

Will the hon. member deny
this principle which has been laid down by one of the highest judges in the Old Country, that there is substantially no difference between a moral claim and a legal claim so far as a government is concerned; that a moral claim necessarily blossoms into a legal claim?

It is a very
poor government that does not look upon any moral responsibility as a legal responsibility once it is shown. One of the things that is troubling me at present is this: Is our appreciation of moral responsibility a dividend of 35 per cent? That is one of the things that is bothering me. If we put it on the basis of moral right, I would like to think that the appreciation this parliament has of a moral obligation is at .least 100 per cent, and that is one of the troubles I have in connection with this matter. It is quite true my hon. friend can find one or two sentences to quote in connection with the war. He can find that in connection with any cross-examination. He will find things here and things there, but if he goes to the argument of Sir Thomas White, if he goes to what he really relied on, what he relied on was the Crerar letter and what was done by the western directors. He was relying upon several things there. He relied, for example, upon the valuation made by my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) and Mr. Haney in connection with one of the worst accounts. He was relying on what he learned from a gentleman whose word, as I said this afternoon, and still say now, he had a right to rely upon, and made no mistake in doing so. That is the real thing.
As bo the legal rights, we are agreed in one sense; there are none at all, but I do think there are special reasons why we should do something for the depositors. I am going to tetll you frankly, Mr. Chairman, I aim in favour of it. I am in favour of something being done for the depositors. I do not like the form of my hon. friends resolution. I do not like the term "current account". I do not know exactly what might not icome under "current account". I would much prefer it covered just depositors, with deposits in open accounts or deposits with notes. I would like to be dear that the only people we are helping are the depositors.

As a matter of fact, the certificate was granted on the 29th of June, 1905. There were, as far as I have been able to find out, serious troubles in the way of the promoters. It was not so much about the matter of incorporation, as it was making an exchange of the assets of the old Home Savings and Loan Company, slow assets, assets o'f a loan company, which ought never to foe made the basis of a bank. recovering from a disastrous real! estate boom which subsequently collapsed, and .my own idea was that it was a very good thing that the Home Savings Company was able to get rid of a good many of their investments which were taken over by the bank. What drew imy attention to it most particularly was something I noticed in Toronto in connection with the criminal proceedings. I thought that went as far as my hon. friend wanted to go.

No, and I brought that up twice in the House since, as my hon. friend will see at page 357 and page 764 of Hansard. What we wanted to find out was how its charter ever came to be granted. before the Court of Appeals that that question was put by one of the judges, and answered by the chief justice in the terms which I stated-that the bank was insolvent when it opened its doors. If the report is right, and if the learned chief justice is right, then we have every reason to pay something to these depositors.
There is another reason why I think we should pay something to these depositors; I am not going to labour this, because I have already said it on more than one occasion. I admit the whole matter could not have been looked after by taking the stand that we were merely interested onlookers. But my view is that the position of , the Finance Minister was not that of merely an interested onlooker; it was his duty to see that the banks were carried on. I really think that my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance made a mistake.
I do not know whether he did himself justice in his evidence at page 575 when he says that while in Montreal seeing Sir Vincent Meredith he made it quite plain to Sir Vincent that he was there merely interested as an onlooker.
I think there is something which everybody affected by the bank's failure has a right to complain of. No Minister of Finance, I submit, Mr. Chairman, discharges his duty by simply being interested as an onlooker when a question so vital and so material to our whole financial policy is at stake. I think on both these grounds I can well support aid to the depositors.
I want to say one thing to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in connection with the little incident this afternoon as to the Senate. I have been approached twice by depositors, and I can tell him very frankly that the advice I gave them was to make sure of this relief by having it included in the estimates. My right hon. friend may think that is odd; I do not. He is going straight against what the Senate has done in the past. If he is looking for a precedent, I would remind him that the Liberal Senate said no to the proposal for relief to the Farmers' Bank depositors,-just such a similar proposition as this.

The grounds
were entirely different in the two cases.

Yes; here you have a nebulous charge against Sir Thomas White; there you had a definite charge of breach of statutory obligations on the part of the Minister of Finance. There is a provision in the Bank Act that so much cash must be put up before a bank can function. Well, what happened in connection with the
Farmers' Bank? No cash was put up, but a note was floated and put back again. The case of the Farmers' Bank depositors was infinitely stronger. I do not want to discuss it. We can find reasons for making nice distinctions here and there in pretty nearly everything, but those are the facts. On that occasion the Senate threw the bill out. My right hon. friend says that he is anxious the Senate should not deal similarly with this measure. I tell him-he may not know it- that his government have done every single thing calculated to make the Senate throw out the bill. I am asked how. Well, it is quite plain. Here is a case of voting money under conditions where there is no room for negligence, no statutory provisions have been offended in the slightest. We have got a law under which it is our business to look after our chartered banks. It is our business to go right into the banks, to know every single thing about each bank, so that we may have knowledge long before the time of failure whether a bank should be allowed to continue business or not. No one that did not require the services of a committee to sit on his sanity would argue that there is not a far greater responsibility for default and negligence where you have the men and the machinery for making sure of these things than where you have not.

During the discussion this

I referred the right hon. gentleman to a vote for $500,000,000 passed in this House in 1918, and I asked him if it was not a fact that this money was passed in the form of a bill instead of being placed in the estimates. He did not agree with me, but I was quite sure I was correct. I find that that was the procedure adopted1 at that time. If you will turn to the Votes and Proceedings of April 6, 1918, page 148, you will find that a resolution was introduced commencing with these words:
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide that a sum not exceeding $500,000,000 be granted to His Majesty towards defraying any expenses that may be incurred by or under the authority of the Governor in Council, during the year ending the 31st day of March, 1919.
For a number of specific purposes. That is the exact procedure the government is following in this case. The record shows that the resolution to which I have referred was reported on the same day. I quote from the Votes and Proceedings:
Ordered, that Mr. Redd (GrenvUle), for Sir Robert Borden, have leave to brine in a bill, No. 38, for granting to His Majesty aid for military and naval defence.
He accordingly presented the said bill to the House, and the same was received and read the first time; and ordered to be read a second time at the next sitting of the House.
This bill, No. 38, was the bill founded on the resolution introduced on April 6, 1918 Now, at page 571 of Hansard of 1918' April 10, I find the heading:
War Grant-$500,000,000
Prime Minister gives Details of War Expenditure and Major General Mewburn Explains Military Estimates.
Then it goes on to say:
Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 38, for granting to His Majesty aid for military and naval defence.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, I proposed the second reading of a bill very much the same as this in February, 1917, and I had then great hope that it would never be necessary to propose in this House a vote for war purposes of so large an amount.
And so on. This shows conclusively not only that a bill was introduced for this purpose in 1918, but that Sir Robert Borden, according to his own statement,
10 p.m. had asked for a large sum of money in the form of a bill in 1917. Now, if you turn to the statutes of Canada for 1918, volumes 1 and 2, you will find chapter 45, An Act for Granting to His Majesty Aid for Military and Naval Defence.

This is the act which was Bill No. 38 to which I referred a moment ago, and it is cited as The War Appropriation Act, 1918. Section 2 says:
From and out of the consolidated revenue fund there may be paid and applied beyond the ordinary grants of parliament a sum not exceeding $500,000,000 towards defraying any expenses that may be incurred by or under the authority of the Governor in Council.

It seems to be as sweeping provision. The House might just as well know what it is doing. This is simply saying that what might well be a matter of accounting becomes a criminal offence and the provision affects a class of people who do not know too much about accounting or about the law,

I think if my hon. friend will read the section carefully he will see that it is well explained. It says:
347a. Every one who, being a bailee of anything capable of being stolen which is under lawful seizure by a peace officer or public officer in the execution of the duties of his office, and being obliged by law or agreement to produce and deliver the thing bailed to such officer or other person entitled thereto at a certain time and place, or upon demand, commits theft and steals the thing bailed if he does not so produce and deliver it; provided that a person accused under this section shall not be convicted if it be proved that the non-production and non-delivery of the thing bailed is not due to any wilful act or omission on the part of the person accused.

It is just exactly as I say. It is a matter of accounting. The man is supposed to have so many bushels of grain and is left in charge of it. If he finds he is one or two bushels short, under thi3 section he is a criminal.

speechtext: This explains itself. It is a section which is in the Imperial Act, 1915. Its purpose is to prevent any miscarriage of justice which might occur owing to the defective nature of the indictment as originally presented and the failure of the prosecuting authorities to apply for the necessary amendment. This gives to the court before trial or at any stage of a trial, when it appears the indictment is defective, power to make such order for the amendment of the indictment, as the court thinks necessary to meet the circumstances of the case, unless, having regard to the merits of the case, the required amendments cannot be made without injustice, and the court may make such order as to the payment of any costs incurred owing to the necessity for amendment as the court thinks fit.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, it is not.

On section 25-Juries in Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The present section 923 reads as follows:
In those districts in the province of Quebec in which the sheriff is required by law to return a panel of petit jurors composed, one-half of persons speaking the English language, and one-half of persons speaking the French language, he shall in his return specify separately those jurors whom he returns as speaking the English language, and those whom he returns as speaking the French language, respectively; and the names of the jurors so summoned shall be called alternately from such lists.
This new section provides that, in any district, the prisoner may upon arraignment move that he be tried by a jury entirely composed of persons speaking the English language, or entirely composed of jurors speaking the French language, and that upon such motion the judge may order the sheriff to summon a sufficient panel of jurors speaking the English or the French language, unless in his discretion it appears that the ends of justice are better served by impaneling a mixed jury. This is suggested and asked for by the provincial authorities at Quebec.

347B. Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a penalty not exceeding four thousand dollars and not less than five hundred dollars or to imprisonment for three y.ars who renders a false or deceptive return with respect to the sale or other disposition of any goods, unless it be proved that there was no intent to deceive.
2. Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a penalty not exceeding four thousand dollars and not less than five hundred dollars or to imprisonment for three years who, being a director, shareholder, manager, officer or employee of any person who renders a false or deceptive return with respect to the sale or other disposition of any goods knowingly makes, permits, concurs in or condones the rendering of the said false or deceptive return.
This amendment is suggested by the Labour department and is the result of the investigation into an alleged combine which recently took place. It appears that companies acting as brokers for certain growers of fruit or other commodities sell these commodities at a certain . price, furnish invoices for smaller amounts and pocket the difference. It is a theft, but it could not be reached under the law as it is. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) may be able to give some instances in that regard.

In the report of the investigation that was made into an alleged combine in the distribution of fruit and vegetables in British Columbia and the western provinces will be found a number of illustrations of what is in mind. The most glaring instance, probably, is mentioned on page 29. The Mayne Island Nurseries forwarded to the Mutual brokers at Vancouver 65 crates of tomatoes, classified as 51 crates No. 1, 10 crates No. 2 and 4 crates No. 3. These were sold by Mutual brokers in Vancouver for these growers over on Vancouver island. They w'ere sold at the following prices: No. 1, $4.50; No. 2, $4; No. 3, $3. When a return W'as made to the growers it was stated that the No. 1 tomatoes had been sold at $3, the No. 2 at $2.25 and the No. 3 at 75 cents.
Criminal Code

These brokers charged the usual commission on the sale, at the rate of 5 per cent, making $8.92 for the 65 crates.
Is that not covered now in the Criminal Code?

The Minister of Justice should answer that; I am told not. Perhaps I had better complete this statement. The commission charged was S8.92. The freight was $5.88 and the Hot House association's charge was 65 cents, a total of $15.45. In short, in addition to that $15.45 the brokers took $103 on 65 crates of tomatoes. Had that been done in the same town or within the same community it could have been regarded as theft, 'but here were these growers 12 m. of tomatoes over on Vancouver island shipping to brokers in Vancouver and expecting the broker to make a proper sale and a- proper return. We have in our possession the original invoices showing exactly what happened. In this case $103 was improperly retained by the brokers. Theft, I call it, but I am told that the Criminal Code makes no provision for such a case. Some law should.

It 'looks like a
clear case of theft, and the Criminal Code should be wide enough to cover it.

The other day the Minister of Railways and Canals had a bill making it an offence to transport liquor under false billing, and so forth. "(2) Every one who by himself, his servant, agent or employee-

with or without the consent or connivance of any servant, agent or employee of any railway, steamship or other transportation company (including any railway or steamship line owned or controlled directly or indirectly by the Crown), knowingly obtains or attempts to obtain the carriage or transportation by such company of any intoxicating liquor into any country, province, district or other place, whether within or without Canada, where the importation or transportation of such liquor is in the circumstances of the case contrary to law:-
